high_priority_articles.title: Europe’s Russia Sanctions Reach China, but the Costs Return Home - China-US Focus
high_priority_articles.summary: Europe’s Russia Sanctions Reach China, but the Costs Return Home  China-US Focus
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Economic warfare in Europe has stranded Russia in the global market, but has yet to produce a reduction in its ambitions. Yet the EU is seeking to expand penalties with no clear outcome in hand. 
EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said he and China’s commerce secretary Wang Wentao had made a “crucial first step” towards rebalancing EU-China trade relations after their talks in Beijing on Oct 9, 2026.
Sanctions imposed in response to a war ultimately face one decisive test: whether they help end it. After four years and twenty-one packages against Russia over Ukraine, Europe can point to mounting economic costs without being able to demonstrate a corresponding change in Moscow’s conduct.
On 23 July, the EU added fourteen entities based in mainland China and Hong Kong to restrictions targeting alleged support for Russia’s military-industrial complex. Beijing answered within a day by placing fourteen European entities under export controls, prohibiting Chinese exporters—and foreign actors handling Chinese-origin goods—from supplying them with controlled dual-use items.
The identical number of targets conceal an asymmetry. A Chinese company denied European dual-use goods may be able to find substitutes elsewhere; a European manufacturer dependent on Chinese-controlled inputs may have fewer alternatives.
Indeed, European firms caught by Beijing’s Announcement No. 30 were soon asking whether they could still obtain the materials their production depended on and whether suppliers further down the chain could continue selling to them at all.
That episode exposes a larger difficulty. The EU’s turn toward Chinese firms is evidence that Brussels is reaching the limits of the targets it can hurt without generating opposition among its own member states. The fallback creates a new exposure: retaliation that can return the costs of Russia sanctions directly to European companies and, through them, to the governments whose unanimous support every subsequent package requires.
Sanctions have raised Russia’s procurement and transport costs, restricted access to Western technology, forced it to sell oil at a discount and damaged its longer-term economic prospects. What they’ve not done is compel Moscow to end or reduce the war, nor moved Beijing’s policy toward Russia by a single inch.
Demertzis and Brookings reach the same weakness by different routes: measures have arrived in stages, allowing Moscow time to adapt, while enforcement gaps, energy exemptions, third-country rerouting and a shadow fleet operating around the oil-price cap have diluted the effect each successive package was intended to produce.
Twenty-one packages in, costs to the EU states continue to scale while leverage does not. Still, Brussels is now preparing to scale again: 1,600 additional individuals and entities allegedly linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex could be proposed, increasing the existing list by about a third. The size makes the question sharper: will another tranche generate leverage that more than twenty previous packages did not, or simply extend a campaign whose marginal returns are becoming harder to identify?
This is where China enters.
The fourteen mainland Chinese and Hong Kong companies were among fifty-one entities added to a list subject to tighter restrictions because of purported support for Russia’s war economy or circumvention of existing controls. Their coercive effect therefore depends on whether the targeted firms need European-origin inputs that cannot readily be replaced.
The political attraction of such listings is easier to see. Chinese companies are often simpler for 27 governments to agree on than targets with powerful constituencies inside Europe. No member state has a national champion behind the Chinese company; fewer domestic lobbies are waiting outside ministries; and the listing can still be presented as action against a declared “systemic rival.” The July measures themselves were calibrated: major Chinese actors were omitted because member states feared retaliation.
That is what sanctions saturation begins to look like. As politically easier targets become scarcer, pressure shifts toward the names nobody around the Council table feels compelled to defend. Sanctions are moving toward the targets political agreement can still reach.
The mismatch runs deeper. Europe built much of its external influence through market access, regulation and standards. That model is strongest when access to the single market is the prize and substitution is costly. It is less suited to a contest in which power can run through control of individual technologies, minerals and components embedded inside another economy’s production chains.
China’s retaliation reverses the direction of European regulatory power. Brussels restricts access to European technology; Beijing asks which European firms depend on Chinese inputs and restricts those instead. Aggregate market size becomes less important than control of the component the other side cannot easily replace.
Washington adds another layer of coercive power that Brussels cannot reproduce. The U.S. can combine tech controls with the reach of the dollar system and secondary sanctions. Europe retains some leverage through its own market and technologies, but not the same financial reach. Against Chinese intermediaries that can replace European suppliers, EU restrictions can therefore impose compliance and commercial costs without producing the behavioural effect Brussels wants.
Beijing’s July response demonstrated the difference in another form: speed. While an EU sanctions package requires unanimous agreement among all 27 member states through extended negotiations, a Chinese export-control listing can be issued through a rapid executive decision. China responded in less than 24 hours; Beijing gave EU officials only about one hour’s warning before announcing its retaliation.
Combined with control over critical inputs, that institutional asymmetry produces escalation dominance. Beijing can identify exposed European entities, prepare its response and activate it before Brussels has begun negotiating its next collective move. The damage can then be concentrated on companies with the least room to adjust.
The exceptional-authorisation clause in Announcement No. 30 adds another lever. An exporter can apply to MOFCOM for permission to proceed in individual cases. That discretion allows Beijing to present the restrictions as calibrated rather than indiscriminate while encouraging affected firms to seek relief through national governments. A retaliatory list can therefore become a wedge between companies and Brussels, and between member states and the institutions that placed those companies in China’s crosshairs.
The political effect is more consequential than the numerical symmetry. The costs Beijing imposes land on member states, each dispute activates domestic lobbies, and each government has to explain the damage to voters—who never approved the exposure in the first place.
The ultimate vulnerability is unanimity itself. Every EU sanction package depends on all governments agreeing. Once retaliation becomes predictable, capitals can look ahead to which of their companies, universities or suppliers might appear on Beijing’s next list. Each exposed constituency creates an argument for an exemption, a narrower designation, a delay or a veto before the next package even reaches agreement.
In other words, China’s answer to the twenty-first package does not have to block the twenty-second to matter. It only has to raise the domestic price of voting for it.
A retaliation doctrine, if Brussels had one, would price that exposure before every vote: which targets carry real coercive weight; which European industries would absorb the response; which components have no reliable second supplier; and which companies would turn to national governments once the bill arrived.
Brussels has never produced a package-by-package account of what these measures achieve. Such scrutiny could expose an uncomfortable reality: the listings may impose greater costs on European firms than the coercive pressure they generate against Russia, while sanctioning a Chinese company can serve political leaders by parading resolve through another package, even when the coercive objective is vague or the expected leverage negligible.
Twenty-one packages in, Brussels is preparing another major expansion while the war continues and retaliation is beginning to travel back through Europe’s own dependencies. The danger is no longer confined to the companies caught in the exchange: once Beijing can turn supply-chain exposure into pressure on the unanimity behind EU sanctions, retaliation begins to erode Europe’s ability to agree to the next package.

high_priority_articles.title: CBAM and EUDR: why European buyers now demand carbon footprints from African exporters - Capmad
high_priority_articles.summary: CBAM and EUDR: why European buyers now demand carbon footprints from African exporters  Capmad
high_priority_articles.full_text:
On 1 January 2026, the operational phase of the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) will start to apply to imports of cement, steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen, with importers required to open a CBAM account once they exceed a threshold of 50 tonnes of goods per year. The European Commission clarified in 2024 that importers or their customs representatives will need a CBAM account number if they cross this threshold as from 1 January 2026. For South African steelmakers, already warned that around 6% of their steel and aluminium exports to the EU, worth some EUR 1.2 billion a year, are directly exposed, this date has become a strategic milestone rather than a mere regulatory constraint. Workshops held with European officials established that the share of South African steel and aluminium exports concerned by CBAM represents about 6% of volumes to the EU, for a value close to EUR 1.2 billion per year.
Beyond carbon‑intensive industries, the new EU rules on deforestation‑free products are making carbon accounting and traceability unavoidable for African exporters of agricultural commodities. As from 30 December 2024, any company placing agricultural commodities such as cocoa from Côte d’Ivoire on the EU market will have to demonstrate that its supplies are legal and deforestation‑free in order to comply with the EU Regulation on deforestation‑free products. For European buyers, this obligation is already flowing through into the technical specifications they impose on African exporters, who must now provide detailed emissions data and forest‑footprint information for each shipment.
Why requirements are shifting toward carbon footprints
The growing demand for detailed carbon footprints does not stem from a generic CSR trend, but from the way Brussels has designed its climate‑related trade instruments. The CBAM regulation, adopted in 2023, creates a carbon tariff on imports of emissions‑intensive products to curb carbon leakage and align non‑EU producers with EU climate standards. To calculate this levy, the European importer needs credible data on the embedded emissions of the imported products; without such data from its African supplier, it risks being charged on the basis of default emission factors that are significantly more punitive.
On the agricultural side, the dynamic is similar but operates through deforestation rather than an explicit tax. EU Regulation 2023/1115 on deforestation‑free supply chains requires that palm oil, coffee, cocoa, rubber, soy, timber and certain derived products be placed on the EU market only after strict due diligence based on traceability data down to the plantation level. In practice, this means that European buyers now expect African exporters to deliver data sets comparable to a carbon footprint: GPS coordinates of plots, land‑use histories and, increasingly, emissions inventories linked to deforestation and processing.
West African cocoa and coffee in the spotlight
In cocoa and coffee value chains, this shift is translating into very specific demands from European roasters, chocolate makers and traders. Research on the Ivorian cocoa sector already shows large variations in traceability across cooperatives and underlines that by late 2024, companies trading these products in the EU will have to prove the legality and deforestation‑free status of their supplies, which implies fine‑grained plot monitoring and information systems aligned with the EUDR.
The reconfiguration does not concern certified chains only. Sector analyses on the EUDR’s impact on African coffee and cocoa trade show that exporters are now being pushed to deploy digital traceability platforms capable of registering plots with GPS data, tracking deforestation with satellite imagery and generating structured due‑diligence documentation for European clients. In practice, the carbon footprint is no longer just a high‑level corporate exercise, but a lot‑by‑lot management tool required upstream by buyers.
How European buyers are rewriting their specifications
Faced with the regulatory calendar, European buyers are translating CBAM and EUDR obligations into very concrete contractual clauses. In the cocoa chain, for instance, cooperatives that have been certified for several years under standards such as Rainforest Alliance or Fairtrade are identified as better positioned to meet these demands, because they already operate farm‑monitoring and data‑collection systems that European buyers seek to rely on. African exporters unable to supply such information risk, in the short term, being pushed toward less demanding markets or losing EU market share altogether.
The requirements tend to cluster around three information blocks that buyers see as inseparable:
- exhaustive mapping of suppliers and subcontractors, down to smallholder level;
- an emissions inventory covering at least energy use, transport and land‑use change;
- the ability to update the carbon footprint annually, in line with the climate‑reporting obligations of large European companies.
In heavy industry, the logic is similar: without verified, auditable emissions factors provided by African companies, European buyers cannot optimise their exposure to CBAM. South African industry players exporting to the EU have been explicitly urged to familiarise themselves with CBAM and prepare to demonstrate that their steel and aluminium exports comply with the emissions standards required in the EU.
African responses still taking shape
Regional initiatives are starting to structure a response, but remain in a ramp‑up phase. The African Organisation for Standardisation (ARSO) has developed a regional cocoa sustainability standard (ARS‑1000) designed to provide traceability and data frameworks compatible with the EU deforestation regulation, in order to help African producers and exporters stay eligible for the EU market. This largely voluntary approach shows that the issue is no longer whether European clients will require detailed carbon footprints, but how African exporters can share the costs of compliance.
In several countries, the supervisory authorities of export crops are gradually aligning with this data‑driven logic. Technical discussions between the European Commission and cocoa authorities in Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire and Cameroon in 2023 focused on traceability systems and on implementing a joint roadmap for the EUDR, with Ghana’s Cocoa Board explicitly seeking support to build traceability capacity and meet the forthcoming due‑diligence requirements. In this context, the carbon footprint is increasingly becoming a shared language between African regulators and European buyers.
The countdown to EU deadlines
In the near term, the dates are known and leave little room for manoeuvre. In the cocoa sector, the 30 December 2024 deadline for the effective application of the deforestation‑free products regulation is forcing a rapid acceleration of plantation mapping and database consolidation for buyers. For industrial sectors covered by CBAM, the transitional period also ends around 2026, when CBAM certificates will become payable and directly linked to reported emissions. Recent Commission communications stress that as from 1 January 2026, CBAM reporting will determine certificate payments and market access for importers exceeding the 50‑tonne threshold for relevant goods.
For African exporters, the immediate question is therefore less about debating the legitimacy of these instruments than about deciding at which level – company, value chain or region – they organise the production and consolidation of carbon data that their European partners now treat as a contractual prerequisite.

high_priority_articles.title: Iran denies role in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, offers mediation
high_priority_articles.summary: Iran on Friday dismissed Saudi Arabia's accusations that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom, with its Foreign Ministry offering to mediate between Riyadh a...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Iran on Friday dismissed Saudi Arabia's accusations that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom, with its Foreign Ministry offering to mediate between Riyadh and the Yemeni group to help ease tensions.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement, reiterating Tehran's offer to act as a bridge between the Houthis and Riyadh.
Baqaei said Tehran "has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities" and remained prepared to use "all its capacities for this purpose at the request of both sides".
The Houthis are part of Iran's so-called "Axis of Resistance," which also includes Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq, all united in opposing Israel.
Tehran has repeatedly denied directing Houthi operations, saying the Yemeni group acts according to its own interests.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets in recent weeks, including vessels in the Red Sea, oil facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last week.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
France, Germany Reach Deal on EU Car Emissions and UK Special Status
Franco-German Agreement on EU Automotive Emissions and Market Access
By Philip Blenkinsop
Background and Proposed Emissions Rules
BRUSSELS, Oct 16 (Reuters) - France and Germany struck a deal on Friday to soften proposed EU car emissions rules and open the door for Britain to be treated as a trusted partner under the bloc's "Made in EU" rules.
The European Commission proposed last year that automakers cut CO2 emissions by 90% from 2021 levels in 2035, with the remaining 10% offset through measures such as the use of low-carbon steel and alternative fuels.
Franco-German Plan Details
Under the Franco-German plan, the 2035 target would be set at 90%, but without the need for additional compensatory measures. The approach is broadly in line with the wishes of German automakers.
European automotive stocks gained after the deal was announced, lifting the STOXX 600 Automobile and Parts Index nearly 2%.
Local-Content and Market Access Provisions
The joint plan also addresses an EU proposal introducing local-content and low-carbon requirements for products bought through public procurement, public auctions or subsidy schemes.
France has pushed for these products to be limited to those manufactured in the European Union. Other EU members, including Germany, argue that countries closely linked to EU automotive supply chains and free-trade-agreement partners should also be included.
Inclusion of the UK and Other Partners
The Franco-German plan says that for the automotive sector, "Made in EU" should cover the EU's 27 countries and other European partners that were part of the EU internal market on January 1, 2020.
That would include Britain, which left the EU single market at the end of 2020.
UK Response and Conditions
An official at British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Downing Street office said inclusion in the "Made in EU" scheme would be good news for Britain's automotive sector. However, he said the Franco-German proposal would need wider European backing and that details had yet to be seen.
The Franco-German plan also says that inclusion should be subject to an agreement on full reciprocity, along with "dynamic alignment with EU conditions for investment from third countries and with EU trade protection measures".
That could mean Britain adopting measures the EU has taken to restrict imports of Chinese-built hybrid and battery-electric vehicles.
Reactions and Controversy
Industry and Political Responses
A GOOD DAY FOR JOBS OR A 'HISTORIC MISTAKE'?
The Franco-German paper also proposed compliance periods spanning multiple years for CO2 emission targets, no revision before 2030 of the utility factor for hybrid vehicles, which measures the share of driving done electrically, and recognition of cars powered by renewable and low-carbon fuels as zero-emission vehicles.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the deal "a good day for motorists and for jobs in Germany, France and Europe".
The deal will not please all automakers. Toyota's European division, which sells cars in Europe from plants in the EU, Britain, Turkey and Japan, said on Thursday that including trusted partners such as Britain, Canada, Japan, South Korea and Turkey would give the EU the scale needed to compete with China.
Turkey's trade minister said this week on a trip to Brussels that trusted partners such as Turkey should not be excluded.
Environmental and Green Group Criticism
Green and environmental groups criticised the emissions proposals.
German Greens lawmaker Swantje Michaelsen said the German government was holding back the automotive industry, with high fuel prices already accelerating demand for EVs.
Anna Krajinska of transport and environment campaign group T&E called the deal a "historic mistake" that would reduce the incentive for industry to invest in EVs.
"German and French political leaders claim they are acting to save jobs, but this may well be the deal that buries Europe’s auto industry," she said.
Next Steps and Outlook
France and Germany still need to convince other EU members and the European Parliament for their plans to enter into force. They are unlikely to reach a final common text before early next year, after an EU-UK summit planned for November 20.
(Reporting by Philip Blenkinsop and Makini Brice. Additional reporting by Alistair Smout, Nick Carey, Rachel More and Kirsti Knolle. Writing by Charlotte Van Campenhout and Philip Blenkinsop. Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria and Mark Potter)

high_priority_articles.title: Houthis’ diverse arsenal fuels renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia
high_priority_articles.summary: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have built a diverse missile and drone arsenal that allows them to sustain attacks against Saudi Arabia and strategic maritime targets, raising concerns...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have built a diverse missile and drone arsenal that allows them to sustain attacks against Saudi Arabia and strategic maritime targets, raising concerns about the duration and intensity of the renewed conflict.
Since early September, the group has struck key oil infrastructure and airports across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh’s airport, which has been targeted 20 times, according to the supplied account. It has also attempted, unsuccessfully, to strike the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The renewed hostilities followed a Saudi bombardment of Sanaa’s airport in July aimed at preventing a Houthi delegation from landing in the Yemeni capital, ending a four-year truce.
April Longley Alley, a Yemen specialist at the Washington Institute think tank, described the subsequent exchanges as a strategy of reciprocal escalation.
“The Houthis framed this campaign as blockade for blockade, airport for airport, escalation for escalation,” she said.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and aerial and maritime drones, giving them multiple options for attacking infrastructure and threatening shipping near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a strategic passage linking the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea.
Their weapons come partly from military stockpiles seized when they captured Sanaa in 2014. Others have been smuggled into Yemen as complete systems or assembled locally from imported components, primarily brought in through the Arabian Sea, said Niranjan BS, a strategic weapons analyst at Jane’s.
According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies’ Military Balance database, the group operates several medium-range ballistic missiles, including systems derived from Iranian designs such as the Kheibar Shekan.
Its shorter-range weapons include the Asef anti-ship missile, derived from Iran’s Khalij Fars missile family, according to the Wilson Center think tank.
The Houthis also possess cruise missiles from Iran’s Quds family. The Quds-4 variant is believed to have a range of about 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles), the Wilson Center said.
Their drone arsenal includes the Waeid-1 and Waeid-2, local copies of Iran’s Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 one-way attack drones, respectively, Niranjan said.
This combination allows the group to vary its attacks and threaten targets at different distances, complicating efforts to neutralize its capabilities.
Iran has provided critical military assistance to the Houthis, particularly through missile and drone technology, according to the Middle East Institute.
In a report, the institute said components manufactured in Iran are smuggled into Yemen by small boats, container ships or across the border with Oman before being assembled locally.
However, analysts caution against portraying the Houthis as a force that simply follows Tehran’s orders.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli analyst specializing in Iran, said the Houthis viewed themselves as partners of Iran rather than proxies.
Iranian personnel linked to the Quds Force, the foreign operations arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, maintain a presence in Yemen and advise the group, Citrinowicz said at a recent conference in Paris. But he said they do not decide Houthi military operations.
In June 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned a man in China suspected of links to the Houthis, accusing him of playing “a key role in procuring materials that enable Houthi forces to manufacture advanced conventional weapons inside Yemen.”
The Houthis have survived years of conflict and sustained air campaigns by Saudi Arabia, the United States and Israel, leaving them experienced in operating under military pressure.
Longley Alley said their ability to withstand previous bombardments suggested that further strikes might not quickly end the confrontation.
“We need to remember with the Houthis that they have withstood punishing air campaigns before, from the Saudis, from the Americans, and from the Israelis,” she said.
“This is a battle-hardened group, and they have much less to lose than the Saudis.”
She added that the Houthis likely believed they could sustain the conflict longer because they were accustomed to absorbing attacks.

New Delhi [India], October 15 (ANI): The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) will come into force on October 20, while India and Canada are targeting the conclusion of negotiations for their proposed trade agreement by the end of 2026, as India seeks to expand market access for exporters amid global trade uncertainties.
According to a presentation by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Thursday, India and Canada are aiming to conclude negotiations for their proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) by the end of 2026.
The fifth round of negotiations between the two countries was held in Ottawa from October 5 to 9, with discussions covering market access for goods and services, investment, rules of origin, intellectual property rights and trade remedies. The next round of talks is planned for early November in New Delhi.
The proposed agreement is expected to strengthen economic ties between the two countries by reducing trade barriers and improving market access for businesses.
Meanwhile, the India-New Zealand FTA, signed in April 2026, will become operational on October 20. The agreement will provide duty-free access to Indian exports entering New Zealand, creating opportunities for sectors such as textiles, leather, footwear, engineering goods and processed agricultural products.
These developments come as India's merchandise exports have recorded growth across several major trading partners during the first half of the current financial year.
According to the Commerce Ministry's trade data, India's exports to the United Kingdom increased to USD 7.32 billion during April-September 2026, from USD 6.83 billion a year earlier. The India-UK trade agreement came into force in July this year.
Exports to China also rose to USD 11.41 billion from USD 8.39 billion, while shipments to the European Union increased to USD 31.92 billion from USD 30.61 billion.
India has earlier concluded FTA negotiations with the European Union, although the agreement is yet to enter into force.
The ministry's presentation further showed that negotiations are underway with several other trading partners, including the United States, Israel, Chile and Peru.
India is also pursuing reviews or upgrades of existing trade agreements with Australia, ASEAN, South Korea and Sri Lanka.
The ongoing negotiations and implementation of new agreements are part of India's efforts to diversify export destinations and secure better market access for domestic businesses amid changing global tariff policies. (ANI)

high_priority_articles.summary: UK to ‘act in lockstep’ with EU over China car tariffs, says minister  The TelegraphFrance drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation  The GuardianUK is prepared to align with EU tariffs on Chinese EVs, minister indicates  POLITICO.euFrance and Germany to allow UK to join EU car policy if it aligns on China tariffs  Financial TimesTariffing Chinese cars risks solving the wrong problem: Executive View  AM-online
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Britain could accept the EU’s demand for tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles, Anas Sarwar, the trade minister, has suggested.
Mr Sarwar told Politico that Britain and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to combat the flood of Chinese imports of electric vehicles (EVs).
His comments were at odds with those of Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, who just a day earlier, reiterated his concern that Beijing could retaliate against British car exports to China.
However, the Financial Times reported on Thursday that France and Germany would now insist that the UK increase tariffs on Chinese cars, meaning manufacturers, such as BYD, Geely and Chery, face levies of up to 45pc.
In return, France would drop its opposition to the UK’s car industry joining the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” scheme. Under the scheme, an EV would qualify for subsidies and public tenders only if at least 70pc of its parts are made within the bloc.
Paris’s previous hard line had left British manufacturers of cars and components fearing they would be frozen out of the Continent, putting up to €80bn (£68bn) of trade at risk.
Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has turned the UK’s inclusion in “Made in Europe” into a key goal for his summit with the EU on Nov 20.
The Financial Times said that if Britain agreed to the tariffs, the “Made in Europe” scheme would be extended to countries that “were part of the EU internal market on Jan 1 2020”.
That would include Britain, but not other countries hoping to join the scheme, such as Japan, Korea and Turkey.
A No 10 official on Thursday welcomed the EU’s apparent willingness to include the UK in the scheme, but did not commit Britain to introducing the tariffs.
“We’ll of course wait to see the detail, and there’s a process still to run in Europe,” he said.
This suggests Britain still sees an opening to continue negotiating.
“The UK and Europe share deep economic and strategic ties,” the official said. “And where we find common cause and approach challenges in a spirit of cooperation, we can create opportunities for businesses and workers on both sides.”
Mr Reynolds had said on Wednesday: “When we make any trade decision in terms of trade defence tariffs in relation to the EU, that’s based on the UK interest – it’s not based on any other country asking for that.”
But on the sidelines of a German-British business summit in London on Thursday, Mr Sarwar said Brussels and London had to “grapple with the challenge that comes from rapid expansion in China”.
“The more that the UK and the EU work together and act in lockstep, the better it is for both the UK and the European Union,” he said.

high_priority_articles.title: BoJ's Ueda signals further rate hikes as underlying inflation nears 2% - Mitrade
high_priority_articles.summary: BoJ's Ueda signals further rate hikes as underlying inflation nears 2%  Mitrade
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Bank of Japan (BoJ) Governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated on Friday that the central bank will continue raising interest rates as underlying inflation approaches its 2% target, noting that financial conditions remain accommodative.
Ueda said economic activity and price developments remain broadly in line with the BoJ's forecasts, while policymakers will discuss at their upcoming meeting whether to revise their assessment of underlying inflation. He added that the timing and pace of future rate hikes will depend on the impact of exchange rate movements, Artificial Intelligence (AI) demand and developments in the Middle East on prices.
The BoJ Governor also highlighted that some global policymakers appeared more optimistic about AI-driven demand than the Japanese central bank had anticipated, although discussions this week did not materially alter its baseline economic outlook.
No big gap in view between what we have assessed on inflationary pressure from AI demand, and what I heard from global policymakers.
I felt that there were more policymakers at this meeting who were somewhat more bullish on ai-demand than we had estimated.
We will continue to raise interest rates as underlying inflation approaching 2%, financial conditions are accommodative.
Economic, price moves roughly in LINE with our forecasts.
Did not hear anything at this week's meetings that deviated from our baseline view.
We will discuss at upcoming meeting whether to tweak our assessment that underlying inflation is approaching 2%.
Timing, pace of future rate hikes will be decided looking at impact of fx, AI demand and Middle East developments on prices.
Haven't been in touch with us treasury secretary bessent since we met in asheville.
As underlying inflation is quite close to 2%, it is becoming more important than before to anchor inflation around our target.
Ueda's remarks had little impact on financial markets, with USD/JPY hovering around 157.95 at the time of writing, virtually unchanged on Friday.
The Bank of Japan (BoJ) is the Japanese central bank, which sets monetary policy in the country. Its mandate is to issue banknotes and carry out currency and monetary control to ensure price stability, which means an inflation target of around 2%.
The Bank of Japan embarked in an ultra-loose monetary policy in 2013 in order to stimulate the economy and fuel inflation amid a low-inflationary environment. The bank’s policy is based on Quantitative and Qualitative Easing (QQE), or printing notes to buy assets such as government or corporate bonds to provide liquidity. In 2016, the bank doubled down on its strategy and further loosened policy by first introducing negative interest rates and then directly controlling the yield of its 10-year government bonds. In March 2024, the BoJ lifted interest rates, effectively retreating from the ultra-loose monetary policy stance.
The Bank’s massive stimulus caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers. This process exacerbated in 2022 and 2023 due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks, which opted to increase interest rates sharply to fight decades-high levels of inflation. The BoJ’s policy led to a widening differential with other currencies, dragging down the value of the Yen. This trend partly reversed in 2024, when the BoJ decided to abandon its ultra-loose policy stance.
A weaker Yen and the spike in global energy prices led to an increase in Japanese inflation, which exceeded the BoJ’s 2% target. The prospect of rising salaries in the country – a key element fuelling inflation – also contributed to the move.

high_priority_articles.title: Wall Street’s Praise for AI Amid Inflation Concerns: Will the Fed Pause Interest Rate Hikes in October? - 36Kr
high_priority_articles.summary: Wall Street’s Praise for AI Amid Inflation Concerns: Will the Fed Pause Interest Rate Hikes in October?  36Kr
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Wash speaks highly of AI, will the Federal Reserve refrain from raising interest rates in October?
This is the first time Walsh has systematically elaborated on his policy stance at a multilateral occasion since he took the helm of the Federal Reserve in May.
On local time October 16, during the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank held in Bangkok, Thailand, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Walsh held a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, covering topics including AI, monetary policy and the global economy.
AI is the most profound economic transformation in a lifetime
Walsh's positioning of AI is extraordinarily rare in its high regard.
He emphasized that AI is the most far-reaching economic transformation he has witnessed in his lifetime.
In his view, AI will first impact the demand side, then unlock productivity dividends on the supply side, and ultimately make the economy more productive and create more wealth.
At present, capital expenditure on data centers, chips and power infrastructure is competing for resources and driving up prices; but in the medium term, AI will bring a positive supply shock.
However, he also warned that "the road to this goal will be very bumpy", and the impact on employment in the next 12 to 18 months remains uncertain.
"I want everyone to feel my optimism, but this optimism carries a serious mission."
To this end, he announced that the Productivity and Employment Task Force established in June will hold its first on-site hearing in the San Francisco Bay Area on November 16.
This is one of five external expert task forces he set up, all of which are expected to submit policy recommendations to the Federal Reserve around the end of the year.
Wei Liang Chang, a macro strategist at DBS Bank, pointed out that Walsh's reaffirmation that AI will boost productivity in the medium term helps ease inflation expectations and reduce market concerns about successive interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, which "will reassure the market".
It is worth noting that recently, affected by concerns that the AI capital expenditure boom may cool down, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index of US stocks has fallen for the seventh consecutive trading day.
Jonas Goltermann, chief markets economist at Capital Economics, warned that more and more signs of the end of the cycle are emerging in US stocks, and a more sustained pullback may occur in the next year or so, accompanied by a decline in US Treasury yields.
He believes that this stock-bond combination exactly matches the market performance that may appear when the AI boom begins to reverse.
Manish Singh, chief investment officer of Crossbridge Capital, further said that although AI demand and long-term opportunities are real, it does not mean that every enterprise building infrastructure can bring satisfactory returns to investors.
"AI may represent the future, but debt repayment is the present."
The interest rate meetings in October and December will be data-dependent
Since the Federal Reserve implemented its first interest rate hike since 2023 in September, the market has been closely watching Walsh's statements on monetary policy.
Meghan Swiber, a US interest rate strategist at Bank of America, said before Walsh's speech that investors are closely watching whether he will "green light" further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.
The answer is: No.
Walsh is unwilling to disclose in advance the possible actions to be taken at the remaining meetings this year.
He emphasized that the Fed's policy conclusions "should not have a preset stance", and it is not appropriate to send signals in advance about what actions may be taken at the remaining meetings this year at the current stage.
When talking about the September interest rate hike decision, Walsh said that the Federal Reserve "clearly demonstrated its determination to achieve price stability" and reduced the degree of monetary easing.
Regarding the next policy path, he said that the trend of the global economy is "generally in line with" the Fed's expectations. There are two remaining interest rate decision meetings in October and December this year, and policymakers will be able to more clearly assess economic output, employment and inflation at that time before determining the monetary policy path.
The timing of this statement is quite sensitive.
On the eve of the speech, the US September CPI and PPI data were released one after another, both exceeding expectations: CPI rose by 3.7% year-on-year, core CPI rose to 2.6% year-on-year, higher than expected for the second consecutive month; PPI soared by 6.3% year-on-year, the largest monthly increase since March 2022.
Despite rising inflation, most Fed watchers still expect the central bank to keep interest rates unchanged this month, postponing the next rate hike to December.
According to the CME "FedWatch Tool", the probability that the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates unchanged in October is 85.1%, and the probability of a cumulative 25 basis point rate hike is 14.9%; the probability of keeping interest rates unchanged in December is 10.8%, and the probability of a cumulative 25 basis point rate hike is 76.1%.
At present, many voting members of the Federal Reserve tend to wait until the December interest rate meeting to take action.
Several senior officials including Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, Governor Christopher Waller, and New York Fed President John Williams have previously sent signals that there is no urgent need to take further action after the September rate hike.
Guy LeBas, chief fixed income strategist at Janney Montgomery Scott, believes that although the price increase of many categories is indeed at a high level, there is no substantial evidence that inflation is accelerating.
Analysts remind that against the background of rapid economic changes, do not overreact to a single data point. Waiting until December to consider raising interest rates will allow the Federal Reserve to have more time to assess the potential trend of prices.
The global economy is in a stage of structural growth
In addition to AI and monetary policy, Walsh also talked about the global economy.
He believes that the global economy is currently in a stage of structural growth, experiencing a round of investment boom that is "not limited to the AI field".
"The economies in almost all regions of the world have shown resilience, which I could not have anticipated five or six months ago."
Walsh attributed this round of investment prosperity to a favorable policy environment, and believes that it is the single most important factor driving the improvement of the global economic development trend.
However, he also admitted frankly that he "may be too sensitive to the shadow left by the global financial crisis".
Since US President Trump launched a war against Iran in February, global energy prices have skyrocketed, triggering Tehran's retaliatory actions against US Gulf allies, plunging the Middle East into crisis.
The rise in oil and gas costs, superimposed on the AI investment boom, has pushed up inflation in many economies including the United States, forcing central banks around the world to raise interest rates.
Walsh pointed out that sustained inflation is a common challenge faced by central banks around the world. At present, most regions of the world are synchronously tightening monetary policy, and "no one can free ride".
It is worth noting that just a few days ago, the IMF released the Global Financial Stability Report, stating bluntly that the global economy is "tilted to the downside in terms of risks".
Chief Economist Silvana Tenreyro warned that the global economy has shown resilience, but this resilience is approaching its limit.

high_priority_articles.title: IMF to Thailand: Shield Indebted Households, Not Fuel Prices, as ASEAN Peers Pull Ahead - Nation Thailand
high_priority_articles.summary: IMF to Thailand: Shield Indebted Households, Not Fuel Prices, as ASEAN Peers Pull Ahead  Nation Thailand
high_priority_articles.full_text:
As ASEAN peers ride the tech boom, IMF says Thailand's 2.1% growth leaves little cushion and urges targeted help for debt-laden households, not fuel caps.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has urged Thailand to support vulnerable, highly indebted households with targeted aid rather than broad energy subsidies, warning that the country’s fiscal buffers are shrinking while regional peers surge ahead on a technology boom.
The recommendation was delivered Thursday (October 15) during a press briefing on the Asia and Pacific economic outlook at the 2026 IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
Thailand is projected to grow just 2.1 per cent in both 2026 and 2027, according to the Fund's Regional Economic Outlook, released at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
That compares with 4.9 per cent for ASEAN as a whole this year, 8.4 per cent for Vietnam and 5.2 per cent for Malaysia. The 2026 figure was raised by 0.6 percentage points from April.
Asked how far household debt is holding back consumption, Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, said successive shocks – the pandemic, the war in Ukraine, tariffs and now the energy shock – had worn down fiscal buffers across the region.
"This is the time to embark upon growth-friendly fiscal consolidation that does not hurt those hit by the shocks," he said.
Governments should use social registries and digitalisation to deliver targeted support, anchored in a well-defined medium-term fiscal framework that reassures investors. The guiding principle, he said, is to "protect people and not prices".
The report details Thailand's own response to the oil shock, which began in February. Bangkok capped fuel prices with subsidies, released petroleum reserves, diversified procurement, restricted some exports, introduced work-from-home arrangements and offered cash transfers and cost-of-living top-ups.
Price-smoothing measures helped contain the pass-through of higher energy costs to inflation, the report said, but the baht came under depreciation pressure, as did the currencies of Indonesia, India and the Philippines, although this has partly eased.
The IMF warned that few such measures across the region are time-bound or clearly targeted and that exit strategies remain unclear in some economies. Broad fuel subsidies and price controls are costlier and weaken incentives to cut demand, it said.
The Fund also flagged longer-term concerns relevant to Thailand.
Its analysis of social safety nets said ageing economies such as Thailand must ensure households have decent incomes in retirement, and that policy should focus on making consumption more resilient among vulnerable, highly indebted households.
It also urged continued work on the "Bangkok Blueprint", the joint IMF, World Bank and Bank of Thailand framework against cyber-enabled financial fraud, which it called a rapidly emerging regional threat.
Growth in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is forecast at 4.9 per cent this year and 4.7 per cent in 2027, upgrades of 0.4 and 0.1 percentage points, respectively, driven largely by technology-related exports and investment.
Vietnam leads at 8.4 per cent in 2026, up 1.3 points. Malaysia is projected at 5.2 per cent and Indonesia at 5.1 per cent. By contrast, the Philippines (3.4 per cent) and Cambodia (3.0 per cent) were cut by 0.7 and 1.0 points.
Srinivasan said ASEAN's energy intensity is about 7 per cent of GDP, higher than Asia's 4 per cent average, leaving some members especially vulnerable if the shock persists. Malaysia and Brunei, as energy exporters, are benefiting.
He urged Indonesia to keep subsidies targeted within its 3 per cent deficit anchor, which markets watch closely, and urged Malaysia to continue fiscal consolidation by broadening the tax base and trimming incentives and subsidies.
On artificial intelligence, he said ASEAN's priority should be skills and lifelong learning.
Asia's growth is projected to ease from 5.0 per cent in 2025 to 4.8 per cent in 2026 and 4.4 per cent in 2027, though 2026 is 0.4 points stronger than April's forecast.
The region will still contribute about two-thirds of global growth – 68 per cent, Srinivasan said.
The IMF credits three forces: adaptation to the oil shock through inventory drawdowns, alternative suppliers and renewables; an AI-driven boom in semiconductors and data centres; and trade that has held up better than feared, helped by surging intra-Asian commerce.
But "resilience is not unlimited", he said, noting that inventories cannot be drawn down indefinitely and fiscal costs are rising.
Risks are tilted to the downside: a prolonged or renewed Middle East escalation, a reassessment of AI profitability, fiscal strains and higher sovereign borrowing costs, and a potentially severe El Niño that could worsen food and energy inflation. Faster AI productivity gains or more predictable trade arrangements could provide upside.
China is forecast to grow 4.5 per cent this year and 4.0 per cent in 2027. Mr Srinivasan said domestic demand remains weak, rebalancing has not materialised and inflation is hovering near deflation.
He called for greater near-term fiscal stimulus and repeated the Fund's call for property-sector support worth about 5 per cent of GDP over three years, including triaging developers.
Korea's growth is forecast to accelerate to 3.3 per cent from 1.1 per cent in 2025, a 1.4-point upgrade. Japan is projected at 0.7 per cent.
Report figures show Korea's current account surplus reaching a record 19 per cent of GDP in 2026, against about 4 per cent for Japan, reflecting Korea's dominance in memory chips.
Sonali Jain-Chandra, the department's deputy director, warned that such concentration heightens vulnerability to any correction in AI demand but said Korea's tight monetary stance remains appropriate, with windfall tax revenues being saved.
India's growth is forecast at 7.0 per cent in 2026 and 2027, up 0.5 points, after a stronger-than-expected first quarter, with medium-term growth of 6.9 per cent.
Srinivasan said the rupee should not be treated as a gauge of economic success and called India's GDP data revisions consistent with good practice.
Bangladesh's growth was cut by 1.1 points to 3.6 per cent. Jain-Chandra said inflation hit 8 per cent in September, tight monetary policy must continue, and revenue, at about 7 per cent of GDP, is among the world's lowest. The IMF is in talks on a new programme requested in May.
On Sri Lanka, she said staff-level agreement on the seventh review was reached in early October, with another review before the programme expires in March. Any follow-on arrangement is the government's choice. She also stressed central bank independence in Nepal.
Pacific island economies are projected to grow 2.6 per cent this year, a 0.2-point downgrade, hit by food and fuel costs. Low-income economies also saw sizeable cuts.
The IMF's analysis of millions of online job postings found employer demand for AI-exposed jobs fell by as much as 10 per cent but has since stabilised, suggesting, Srinivasan said, that AI is "reshaping" the labour market rather than eliminating work.
The region needs nearly 150 million jobs over the next decade, the Fund's blog said.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia has publicly accused Iran of encouraging Yemen's Houthis to attack the kingdom, saying it violates a 2023 diplomatic deal it reached with Tehran to smooth over relations.
"We think the escalation by the Houthis at this later stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," Rayed Krimly, deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry, told journalists on Friday, in a rare public statement.
Krimly’s comments mark the first public signal that the war in Yemen has put pressure on Riyadh’s ties to Tehran.
Krimly said that the Houthis’ attacks were a breach of a March 2023 rapprochement that was brokered by China under which Saudi Arabia and Iran resumed diplomatic relations. At the time, the agreement was seen as a sign of China’s successful foreign policy. Beijing has good ties with both Tehran and Riyadh.
“[Iran] continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and in violation of its commitments in the Beijing agreement,” Krimly said.
The agreement was generally understood to include a commitment from Tehran to restrain the Houthis in support of a United Nations-backed ceasefire.
Saudi Arabia has faced multiple attacks since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, putting pressure on the delicate rapprochement the two countries struck. Saudi Arabia even joined the US in launching some strikes on Iran earlier this year in retaliation, although it later pivoted to mediation.
Despite the tensions, Saudi Arabia has maintained diplomatic engagement with Iran.
Pressure
Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan held a phone call with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi this week. Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia’s ambassador to Iran publicly attended Araghchi’s sister’s funeral.
But the kingdom is now reeling from intense Houthi missile and drone strikes that have targeted civilian infrastructure including airports, oil facilities and the corporate headquarters of Aramco.
The Houthis garnered support in the Muslim world for attacking vessels linked to Israel and the US after 7 October 2023, when Israel responded to a Hamas-led attack by launching a war on Gaza, deemed a genocide by the UN, human rights groups and genocide scholars. But the group’s attacks on civilian sites in Saudi Arabia have sparked backlash.
Video footage from the Houthis' Saturday strike on Riyadh airport showed Umrah pilgrims absorbing a strike that killed at least 13 people and severely wounded hundreds more.
Saudi Arabia led an intervention into Yemen’s civil war in 2015. The kingdom launched a devastating bombing campaign against the Houthis that contributed to what the UN called the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.
In 2022, Yemen’s internationally recognised government, whose biggest backer is Saudi Arabia, reached a ceasefire with the Houthis. The agreement ushered in a fragile truce that endured even during US and Israeli strikes on the Houthis.
The Houthis have received arms, training and intelligence from Iran.
The war in Yemen erupted again after Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July to prevent a plane carrying Houthi officials from landing. Middle East Eye reported that Iranian, Syrian and Hezbollah military advisors were on board, along with weapons systems.
The Houthis declared a blockade against Saudi shipping as a result, and launched a lightning offensive down the Red Sea coast last month, which the kingdom and its Yemeni allies have struggled to counter. They have also launched hundreds of missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.

high_priority_articles.title: Trump: Israel helping Saudi Arabia against Houthis, normalization closer than ever - Israel National News
high_priority_articles.summary: Trump: Israel helping Saudi Arabia against Houthis, normalization closer than ever  Israel National News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump said Friday that Israel has been providing assistance to Saudi Arabia in its confrontation with the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, while expressing optimism about the prospects for diplomatic normalization between Jerusalem and Riyadh.
Speaking with reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked whether Saudi Arabia should accept Israeli assistance in its campaign against the Houthis.
"Yeah, I do. I think they will. Israel has been very helpful to Saudi Arabia," the President responded.
Trump's remarks suggested that cooperation between Israel and Saudi Arabia has continued despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations between the two countries.
Asked whether Saudi Arabia's potential entry into the Abraham Accords was once again under consideration, Trump indicated that the prospects for an agreement had improved.
"Yeah, I think so. Maybe more than ever. The Abraham Accords is one of our great achievements. But Saudi Arabia is very happy to have Israel's support and our support," he said.
The United States has sought to bring Saudi Arabia into the Abraham Accords, the normalization framework established during Trump's first administration.
Israel and Saudi Arabia appeared to be making progress toward a US-mediated diplomatic agreement before Hamas launched its October 7, 2023, terrorist attack against Israel.
Following the massacre, the Saudi government suspended the American-backed normalization initiative, leaving the proposed agreement unresolved.
Trump has subsequently linked the prospect of closer US-Saudi nuclear cooperation to Riyadh's willingness to establish official diplomatic relations with Israel.
In July, Washington and Riyadh announced a nuclear cooperation agreement known as a 123 Agreement.
Two days after the agreement was signed, Trump told reporters that Saudi participation in the Abraham Accords was a requirement for proceeding with the arrangement.
“I just say that in order to do it, they have to be a member of the Abraham Accords, which have been very successful. But it's time now that they do it," Trump said at the time.
His latest comments indicate that he continues to view Saudi-Israeli normalization as a central objective of American diplomacy in the Middle East, alongside cooperation against Iranian-backed forces in the region.

Abstract:
Under the Animal Health Protection Act (7 U.S.C. 8301et seq.) the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) of the U.S. Department of Agriculture is authorized, among other things, to prohibit or restrict the importation and interstate movement of animals and animal products to prevent the introduction into and dissemination within the United States of livestock diseases and pests. To carry out this mission, APHIS regulates the importation of animals and animal products into the United States. APHIS' Veterinary Services is the program responsible for regulating these importations.
The regulations in 9 CFR part 93 contain, among other things, provisions that address the risk that imported bovines (cattle or bison) may introduce or disseminate brucellosis or bovine tuberculosis (TB) within the United States. In 2020, APHIS amended its import regulations to establish a system to classify foreign regions at designated status levels for bovine TB and brucellosis; to establish provisions for modifying the TB or brucellosis classification of a foreign region; and establishing conditions for the importation of cattle and bison from regions with the various classifications.

Dollar-Yen Softens to Upper 157 Range as Fed Chair Remarks Cool Year-End Rate Hike Expectations
The dollar-yen pair softened in foreign exchange markets on the 16th, sliding to the 157.80 level. Fed Chair Warsh offered no clear directional signal on future monetary policy, causing expectations for additional rate hikes this year to recede. Dollar selling prevailed as U.S. long-term yields declined.
In Tokyo trading, the pair climbed to 158.18 in the morning before grinding lower through the afternoon, touching 157.79 at one point. Speaking in a conversation with IMF Managing Director Georgieva, Fed Chair Warsh stated, "I hold no preconceptions about the FOMC's conclusions. I do not think it is appropriate to say at this point what we will do at meetings later this year." While some had anticipated hawkish remarks on inflation after the previous day's U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) came in above market expectations, Warsh ultimately showed no inclination to lean toward additional rate hikes.
In New York trading, dollar-yen briefly climbed to 158.34, but reversed to 157.70 as Warsh's remarks circulated. The pair later stabilized as dollar selling paused amid a rise in U.S. long-term yields tied to higher crude oil prices, finishing the session at 157.99.
EUR/USD rose to $1.1262 before retreating to $1.1213, closing at $1.1237. EUR/JPY fell from 177.90 to 177.38.
Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told the Upper House Budget Committee in the afternoon that she intends to "work toward maintaining orderly currency markets" while communicating with the U.S. Treasury Department, though the market reaction was limited.
At the National Association of Shinkin Banks convention, Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida read remarks on behalf of BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda, stating that "underlying inflation exceeding 2% cannot be tolerated," signaling a continuation of rate hikes. Market participants largely interpreted this as maintaining the BOJ's existing stance of assessing the pace of future hikes while monitoring inflation trends, and it was noted as a yen-supportive factor.
Hiroshi Suzuki, chief FX strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, noted: "We are currently in a wait-and-see phase on monetary policy in both Japan and the United States. Financial market attention is shifting toward European developments and trends in tech company corporate bonds."
From a technical standpoint, the 200-day moving average near 158.57 is seen as overhead resistance, while the 25-day moving average near 157.49 is viewed as downside support. With U.S. midterm elections approaching in November, some market participants suggest this is not the time to take aggressive positions.

Uncertainty Surrounding U.S. Monetary Policy Weighs on Dollar
The U.S. CPI released on the 14th exceeded market expectations, briefly heightening caution over additional rate hikes. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield spiked to the 5.32% level at one point. However, with Fed Chair Warsh showing no inclination toward further tightening, the probability of an additional rate hike at the October Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting declined.
Market participants increasingly see a challenging environment for discerning the direction of monetary policy in both Japan and the United States. While the BOJ has signaled its intention to continue raising rates, the Fed has maintained its data-dependent approach, leaving dollar-yen without clear directional conviction.
Crude oil price movements are also influencing currency markets. Front-month WTI futures traded in the low $97 per barrel range, below the previous day's settlement of $97.97. With the rise in oil prices pausing, upward pressure on U.S. rates through inflation expectations has eased, contributing to a slowdown in dollar-buying momentum.
Going forward, the focus shifts to U.S. economic indicators, remarks from Fed officials, and the BOJ's policy management. With U.S. midterm elections also approaching in November, a wait-and-see stance is likely to intensify in currency markets for the time being.

high_priority_articles.title: Singapore key exports jump by higher-than-expected 68.4% in September, led by non-electronics - The Business Times
high_priority_articles.summary: Singapore key exports jump by higher-than-expected 68.4% in September, led by non-electronics  The Business Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Electronics exports continue to surge on AI-related demand, but economists warn that this will soften in 2027
[SINGAPORE] The Republic’s non-oil domestic exports (NODX) surged 68.4 per cent year on year in September, more than double the 32.2 per cent consensus forecast of private-sector economists in a Bloomberg poll.
Driven by non-electronics NODX, the latest showing also extended August’s revised 46.1 per cent expansion, Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) data showed on Friday (Oct 16).
This was the strongest print since February 1980, said OCBC chief economist Selena Ling.
Electronics exports growth remained robust, and watchers agreed that the trend should hold in the near term. But they noted that artificial intelligence-related tailwinds will begin to soften in 2027.
In the first nine months of 2026, NODX grew 27.6 per cent year on year.
Underpinned by this robust year-to-date growth, RHB upgraded its full-year NODX to 25 per cent, from 15.5 per cent.
Ling also observed upside risk to OCBC’s full-year forecast of 20 per cent, even if growth in the final quarter moderates to 11.5 per cent on year, considering base effects.
Non-electronics shipments expanded 54.2 per cent on the year in September, significantly higher than August’s 11.9 per cent, which EnterpriseSG primarily attributed to “the lumpy exports of structures of ships and boats”.
But it did not cite the year-on-year growth rate, “as the exceptionally high percentage growth reflects a low base effect in the same period last year”.
Other key drivers of the non-electronics NODX increase were non-monetary gold (124.3 per cent) and specialised machinery (50.4 per cent).
Meanwhile, electronics exports soared 107.6 per cent on a yearly basis in September, supported by robust AI-related demand. This was down from 131.6 per cent in the preceding month.
The growth was mainly led by disk media products (312.4 per cent), integrated circuits (74.7 per cent) and PCs (149.5 per cent).
Still growing
Electronics NODX grew 89.5 per cent year on year so far in 2026; and non-electronics, 8.2 per cent, Ling noted.
She said: “Despite recent equity market volatility in AI-related names, fundamentals such as earnings growth and order books, as well as domestic leading indicators such as the manufacturing and electronics Purchasing Managers’ Indexes, remain healthy.”
She thus believes that near-term export momentum should hold up, even as headline NODX growth moderates on higher base effects.
Said DBS senior economist Chua Han Teng: “Notably, electronics PMI sub-indices such as new export orders, and order backlogs have remained on an uptrend, while inventories are drawn down.”
RHB group chief economist Barnabas Gan and associate research analyst Laalitha Raveenthar expect that resilient AI demand and the ongoing tech upcycle should underpin export momentum through year-end.
While the three-month moving average growth of several key electronics products moderated in September, electronics exports remained robust, suggesting that underlying technology demand remains firm despite some moderation in product-level growth momentum, they said.
Global semiconductor sales, which reportedly reached a record US$159.7 billion in August 2026, also point to the broader semiconductor cycle remaining supportive, the pair added. “The global AI investment cycle is expected to remain a key growth support, even as AI-driven growth moderates from its exceptional pace.”
Eventual slowdown
Still, RHB’s duo flagged a quarter-on-quarter manufacturing output contraction in the third quarter, reversing from the second quarter’s expansion. While this does not necessarily signal a turning point, they said that the pullback warrants caution over the durability of growth in the coming quarters.
Economists cautioned that AI-led demand looks set to moderate in the longer term.
Ling pointed out: “The risk is that the current investment cycle begins to mature into 2027.”
Private-sector economists believe that AI-related spending will ease from the high levels in 2026, especially in the second half of next year, weakening demand for Singapore’s exports.
RHB said that MAS highlighted the possibility of an “AI infrastructure credit shock”, where weaker-than-expected AI monetisation could prompt hyperscalers to pare back capital expenditure, triggering a repricing of debt-financed AI investments.
“This could tighten financial conditions, delay projects along the AI supply chain and create a self-reinforcing downturn in investment and global growth,” the RHB duo added.
Standard Chartered’s chief economist Edward Lee and senior economist Jonathan Koh explained: “A sharper or more sustained correction in AI-related assets could pose an additional downside risk if tighter financing conditions cause technology firms to reassess AI capex.”
UOB associate economist Jester Koh added that higher global interest rates that could instill a degree of caution among firms about undertaking new investments.
Beyond technology-related risks, economists also named geopolitical tensions, crude oil price volatility, trade restrictions and a weaker US economy as key headwinds.
Breakdown by market
In September, key exports to Singapore’s top 10 markets – except India – rose. NODX to India fell 5.6 per cent, in a turnaround from the 23.6 per cent growth recorded in August.
UOB’s Koh said: “By destination, electronics NODX to markets deeply embedded in the semiconductor value chain remained robust.”
Key exports to the US rose 73.2 per cent year on year; the rise for Taiwan was 96.9 per cent, and for South Korea, 96 per cent.
Key exports to the EU grew 11.3 per cent in September, reversing from the 1.7 per cent fall in the previous month. In September, the EU was the only market out of Singapore’s top 10 to record a decline in NODX.

At least five people have been killed in the vicinity of the al-Maashiq presidential palace in Yemen’s port city of Aden after Houthi missile strikes.
Yemeni health minister says five people were killed and 16 others injured in the Houthi missile attack that targeted the al-Maashiq Presidential Palace in Yemen’s Aden on Thursday.
The Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said in a social media post on Thursday that Houthis had targeted the al-Maashiq presidential palace with five missiles.
The government says the prime minister and other officials are safe, but two of his bodyguards were killed in the attack.
Plumes of smoke could be seen rising from the vicinity of the palace.
Al Jazeera correspondents reported earlier on Thursday that there were explosions near the palace.
The palace is considered the headquarters and the seat of power for the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, said the attacks on the headquarters of the internationally recognised government are the “first of their kind” by the Houthis.
“This is an indication that the escalation is going to intensify between both sides,” Mawry said, adding that fears are now growing inside the country of “an all-out civil war” that could potentially drag in other regional powers besides Saudi Arabia.
The attack in Aden came as fighting between the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), and Saudi-backed forces intensified in Taiz, which is effectively under siege by the Houthis.
Controlling Taiz, Yemen’s third city and the broader Taiz governorate, in the southwest of the country would ensure control over the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait for either side.
Forces allied with the Yemeni government said they are repelling a Houthi attack on Dhubab airport.
The pro-government Homeland Shield Force said in a statement that they are, along with the Southern Giants Brigades, securing the airport in the coastal city of Dhubab in Taiz governorate.
Aid agencies say the escalating violence in Taiz is pushing the healthcare system towards breaking point.
On Sunday, the Ministry of Public Health warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” there.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition says Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has come under at least 20 Houthi attacks over the past 11 days with dozens of other airports, oil facilities and ports also targeted.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the alliance, released footage showing strikes on the main airport with passengers seen fleeing for safety, during a news conference in the Saudi capital,
The coalition says the Houthi attacks have killed 17 people and injured more than 300.
Al-Maliki also accused the Houthis of obtaining ballistic missiles from other countries in the region.
Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said the Saudi-led coalition’s news conference was intended as a response “to some of the, perhaps, military and security failures”.
“There’s kind of an image problem there because this is maybe affecting the perception of Saudi deterrence, the fact that missiles are getting through,” he told Al Jazeera.
Elmasry said the Houthis also have an image crisis, with the global community viewing their actions as “reprehensible, in particular these targeting civilian infrastructure”.
