high_priority_articles.summary: Inconclusive sparring at EU summit puts budget timeline into question  EuronewsGermany pours cold water on Irish-drafted EU budget proposals  Irish IndependentFrance's Macron warns EU leaders they need budget deal before year-end, say diplomats  ReutersShorten EU budget to 3 or 4 years, Cyprus president tells POLITICO  POLITICO.euCzech Prime Minister Babis rails against EU budget support for Ukraine  The Kyiv Independent
high_priority_articles.full_text:
EU leaders stuck to their red lines on the next long-term budget at Thursday's summit, with several now rejecting the presumed December deadline. Council President António Costa is now expected to take over the negotiations, with a new compromise due in a few weeks.
EU leaders have refused to budge on the bloc’s next long-term budget and openly cast doubt on whether a deal can be sealed by the end of the year, a slippage that would mean significant delays and a collision with a string of national elections.
Until now, capitals were committed to reaching a final agreement by December 2026. But at Thursday’s summit in Brussels, where talks dragged longer than expected, a growing number of governments are asking whether that is really necessary.
"We are not reaching an agreement this month. Not next month. I don’t know even if it’s possible to reach an agreement before the end of the year," said caretaker Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. "I think we are not in a hurry."
For months, European Council President António Costa has repeated that leaders must unanimously agree the next seven-year budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), by December at the very latest.
If talks spill into 2027, he warns, there will not be enough time to complete the complex legislative work needed to get the budget up and running by 1 January 2028.
Following the inconclusive summit, where the Irish presidency’s compromise proposal to cut the overall volume by €141 billion was largely rejected, Costa will take over the negotiations, which was largely expected.
The European Council President is due to present a new negotiating proposal in a few weeks, which is bound to follow a completely different logic from the Irish one. EU leaders have been called in for a special summit on 26 November.
In particular, Costa's proposal is due to keep the national contributions low, a new package of EU-wide taxes to finance the budget, and maintain sufficient flexibility for unforeseen expenses, a budget line the Irish proposal significantly cut down.
Already before the summit, the draft joint conclusions were watered down concerning the deadline, softening language that explicitly set out “the aim of reaching a final agreement by the end of the year.”
By contrast, the final language says that "an agreement before the end of 2026 would allow for the adoption of legislative acts in 2027, which is necessary to ensure that EU funding reaches beneficiaries without interruption in January 2028."
Speaking before the summit, several leaders made clear that they do not feel bound by an end-of-year timeline, as it would be extremely difficult to explain to their domestic audiences that they accepted a bad deal because of an artificial deadline.
"The date cannot become more important than the content," Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told the Senate on Wednesday.
"We will not sign an agreement that is not advantageous to us just to meet a deadline. We will sign an agreement only when it is right for Italy."
There is, however, no consensus on what a “good deal” looks like. Every government wants to take as much as possible from the EU budget while paying in as little as possible.
The main battle line runs between two camps: the so-called “frugals,” a German-led coalition of six net contributors pushing for steep cuts to the overall volume, and the Friends of Cohesion, a 17-strong bloc of southern and eastern countries fighting to preserve traditional funding programmes for the poorest regions.
But the camps are not monolithic. Some Friends of Cohesion, like Spain and Italy, have a vested interest in agricultural funds. Others, like the Baltic states, want to boost defence spending due to their proximity to Russia.
Among the frugals, Germany and Sweden are seen as the most radical, while Finland is keen on farming subsidies. France, the bloc’s second-largest economy, has yet to pick a side, trapped between its European ambitions and a runaway budget deficit.
Belgium and Luxembourg are somewhere dithering between the factions.
"In the end, we need a good Multiannual Financial Framework. So, of course, everyone wants to make speed. But it’s more important to have a good deal than a bad deal," Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said.
In other words, the red lines are so entrenched, and the room for compromise so slim, that a landing zone currently looks like a mirage.
In Brussels circles, deals on sensitive topics are only struck under intense time pressure, because neither side feels compelled to make concessions until the last minute. Signalling that one does not feel bound by a timeline may therefore be a negotiating tactic to stand one’s ground.
For EU officials, even more worrying than the potential delay to funding programmes are the string of elections due in 2027 in France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Estonia, Slovakia and Greece. Some fear that if no deal is reached by the end of this year, it could slip to autumn 2027.
Paris is a particular concern. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is currently the favourite to win the presidential race, and she has promised to cap France’s contribution at €5 billion a year, a sharp cut from the current level of around €8 billion.
Meanwhile, elections in Spain, where voters go to the polls on 29 November, and Sweden, which voted in September, "are likely to create some issues", said Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides.
Christodoulides reiterated the need to reach an agreement by the end of the year. He is one of the few EU leaders still saying so.

Investors reassessed Federal Reserve policy expectations as officials signaled little urgency to raise interest rates further, while concerns about an artificial intelligence-driven stock market correction unsettled financial markets.

The British pound climbed 0.31% to $1.3314 and gained 0.63% over the week. The dollar fell 0.25% against the Swiss franc to 0.8246, leaving it down 0.67% for the week as demand for defensive assets supported Switzerland's currency.
Market pricing reflected a shift in expectations for US monetary policy. According to the CME FedWatch Tool, investors assigned an 83% probability to the Federal Reserve leaving rates unchanged later in October, compared with 49% a month earlier.
Matt Weller, global head of market research at StoneX in Michigan, highlighted the unusual relationship between the dollar and technology stocks during the week's market volatility.
"What I found most interesting today and more broadly this week, is how closely the dollar has been tied to the AI trade. Usually if we see a sell off in tech stocks you would expect the greenback to get a safe-haven bid. We are seeing an element of that into bonds, but the dollar is actually falling."
Technology shares suffered substantial declines as investors questioned whether data center operators could generate sufficient profits to service their debts. The pressure extended into parts of the credit market, raising concerns about the financial risks associated with heavy investment across the artificial intelligence supply chain.
Some relief emerged after CoreWeave-related assets recovered modestly on Thursday. ING's October 16 foreign exchange analysis attributed the rebound partly to comments from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who said CoreWeave's financial strength was improving and its cost of capital was declining.

high_priority_articles.title: Who decides what constitutes dangerous artificial intelligence: the state or Nvidia? - Tomorrow's Affairs
high_priority_articles.summary: Who decides what constitutes dangerous artificial intelligence: the state or Nvidia?  Tomorrow's Affairs
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Jensen Huang, the founder and chief executive of Nvidia, the world’s leading artificial-intelligence chipmaker, said in an interview with Bloomberg Television on 14 October that Nvidia would suspend deliveries to any customer whose use of artificial intelligence would harm people.
He was responding to a hypothetical question and added that the decision would be preceded by a conversation with the customer, acknowledging that there are limits to a supplier’s right to impose its values on others.
Nvidia generated $89 billion in revenue from data-centre equipment alone in the quarter ended 26 July, and its chips power most of the world’s artificial-intelligence systems.
Any customer denied deliveries would struggle to find a replacement in the quantities required, so such a decision could effectively halt its development.
Nvidia is now linking the sale of its computing equipment to the development of safety tools and support for researchers examining AI safety.
Huang’s willingness to judge the harms caused by the use of its chips would extend that influence to the selection of eligible customers.
The company would therefore independently decide under which conditions the technology may spread, while its director claims that the industry does not need new laws.
China is the strongest test of Huang’s promise, as there is already a case there in which the state concluded that the sale of Nvidia’s chips posed a danger.
Washington has been restricting exports of the most advanced chips to China since 2022, fearing that they will be used to strengthen its military and to develop its own artificial intelligence capabilities.
In May 2025, Huang called the controls a failure, arguing that they merely help China’s competitors grow stronger.
His argument is supported by the latest data from research company IDC, which shows that Nvidia’s share of the Chinese market for artificial intelligence chips fell in the first half of 2026 to 34 per cent, while China’s Huawei reached 28 per cent.
Meanwhile, Washington relaxed but maintained controls. On 8 December 2025, President Donald Trump announced that Nvidia could sell H200 chips, the previous generation of its most powerful processors, to selected Chinese customers.
On 13 January 2026, the Department of Commerce mandated that each request be considered individually, with security requirements and mandatory chip testing in the United States.
Nvidia received the first licence, for limited quantities and specified customers, in February.
China shows how Nvidia reacts when the threat assessment comes from outside and starts to cost it money
The chips are manufactured in Taiwan, so before being shipped to China they must pass through the United States, where they are subject to a 25 per cent tariff. The US government thus takes a quarter of the value of each sale.
Beijing has not made it easy either, restricting domestic companies from buying American chips to encourage Huawei and other Chinese manufacturers.
That is why Nvidia delivered only a fraction of the approved quantities by the end of July, and those sales brought in less than 1 per cent of its data-centre equipment revenue.
Restrictions cost Nvidia money even when they are relaxed. In the same report, the company took a $400 million write-down because of an inventory of H200 chips that it could not sell.
When the US government banned the sale of H20 chips, a model made specifically for the Chinese market, in April 2025, Nvidia was left with stock it could no longer sell and recorded a loss of $4.5 billion.
Export controls concern the military and technological power of another country, and Huang’s October pledge concerns the harmful use of products, so the two cases are not quite the same.
China, however, shows how Nvidia reacts when the threat assessment comes from outside and starts to cost it money.
The company has the right to challenge government policy, but the argument that the restrictions do not work simultaneously protects its access to one of the world’s largest markets.
Huang’s announcement therefore carries no real weight until it is clear how much loss Nvidia would accept if the harmfulness of using its chips were decided by someone outside the company.
On 15 September, at the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, the annual gathering of software company Salesforce, Huang said the industry “doesn’t need new laws or new regulations” and that AI security is an “engineering problem”.
Pope Leo XIV responded on 28 September at a press conference on the plane, on his way back from France.
He said he had read Huang’s claim that he had found a way to place technical limits on artificial intelligence and pointed out that this was the same man who said it did not need any restrictions or government regulation. Nvidia presented precisely that control system on the same day.
The Pope’s remark draws on the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, his letter on artificial intelligence published in May.
In it, he warns that decision-making is being concentrated in the hands of a small number of technology companies and insists that affected communities have a say. He specifically calls for legal frameworks and independent oversight.
The dispute with Huang thus centres on who sets the limits of artificial intelligence: the companies that create it, or the society that lives with its consequences.
Huang does not reject all state control, however. In a conversation with American journalist Ezra Klein at the end of September, he said that AI companies should not be exempt from competition laws or from responsibility for damage caused by their products.
He also supported special rules where needed, for example for autonomous cars.
The more secure agents become, the more companies will deploy them, and most of these agents will run on Nvidia chips
He draws the line at the models themselves, insisting that companies should decide whether a new artificial intelligence system is safe enough to enter the market.
Nvidia’s system is designed for so-called AI agents, programmes that autonomously perform a range of tasks, from sending emails to working with confidential company data.
The OpenShell programme determines which data and systems the agent is allowed to access, with rules set by the company that uses it.
Sentry, a dedicated hardware watchdog, monitors the agent’s operation and, according to Nvidia, can stop it within milliseconds if it tries to exceed the permitted limits.
The more secure agents become, the more companies will deploy them, and most of these agents will run on Nvidia chips. Protection is therefore a new way for Nvidia to sell more equipment.
Part of that offering is open. The OpenShell is publicly available and can be adapted to third-party equipment.
Sentry, however, runs only on Nvidia’s BlueField-4 hardware. A company that builds protection around both tools will be able to move software easily, but not monitoring, so switching to another supplier will become increasingly expensive as it relies more on Nvidia’s equipment.
Nvidia announced that it will provide British artificial intelligence security researchers with computing capacity worth an estimated $250 million, or about $50 million per year, over the next five years.
That funding will remain within Nvidia’s system, as universities gain the right to use the computers of its British partners, equipped with its chips.
Among the first users will be the BOLD laboratory at Oxford and the SOFAIR laboratory, UK national AI research laboratory.
The announcement explicitly states that researchers will also work with the OpenShell and Sentry tools.
In the coming years, British security experts will, at Nvidia’s expense, examine and improve the very protections that Nvidia sells to companies
In the coming years, British security experts will, at Nvidia’s expense, examine and improve the very protections that Nvidia sells to companies.
Universities will receive equipment for costly experiments that they could hardly fund themselves, and Nvidia will gain the opportunity to establish its solutions as a common benchmark for assessing the safety of artificial intelligence.
Key terms have not yet been agreed. Nvidia has not announced which partners will provide the services, how the computers will be organised, under what commercial terms, or how much individual universities will receive.
Those contracts will also depend on whether researchers are allowed to freely publish findings that are unfavourable to the donor.
Part of the programme could also work against Nvidia’s interests. The SOFAIR laboratory investigates new ways of building artificial intelligence, with the aim that development does not depend on a few large companies.
Nvidia’s funding could therefore support technologies that may one day reduce dependence on its products, provided the results can be used on other organisations’ equipment.
The British package seems more modest than the American one. On 8 October, Nvidia announced $1 billion over five years for US science, health, energy and advanced computing research – four times more than for Britain.
However, Britain is not tied to a single supplier. Nvidia’s main competitor, AMD, announced in June that it would invest up to two billion pounds over five years in British computing infrastructure and scientific collaboration, and it is also participating in Oxford’s BOLD laboratory.
This freedom of choice has its price, because every programme written for one set of equipment must be adapted before switching to another, and that price increases with each year of operation on the same chips.
The British government has its own institute to evaluate artificial intelligence, but it has no authority to examine systems without the consent of the companies that develop them.
The AI Security Institute was founded in November 2023, at the first world summit on artificial intelligence safety at Bletchley Park, under the name AI Safety Institute.

high_priority_articles.full_text:

16 Oct 2026, 11:32 GMT+10
            
New Delhi [India], October 16 (ANI): Non-tariff barriers remain the single biggest obstacle in trade ties between India and China, Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman said on Friday, pointing out that an expanding trade imbalance continues to weigh heavily against the country despite years of bilateral engagement.
The Minister made these observations during an interactive session with Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council on 'India's economic edge', held on the sidelines of the World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.
Addressing the trade friction with Beijing, Sitharaman said that, "So non-tariff barriers are the biggest hurdle in the trade between India and China. That is one, and second, if the approach globally that you see today, where imbalance is huge, countries impose tariffs and say, 'no, we cannot sustain this imbalance, either you correct it or else we are going to be very punitive on you', that approach we have never taken."
Sitharaman mentioned that with China, the trade balance is against India' and it is growing exponentially. "The trade imbalance is something which we have been talking about with China now for several years. We are denied market access, even for those goods for which there are immense market opportunities in China."
She noted that Indian products face persistent roadblocks across key sectors despite proven global competitiveness.
"We are global leaders in generic drugs, bovine meat, vegetables and perishables and very many such goods which have huge potential in China. I would think a decade has gone by, consistently putting up a case for market access for Indian products. But non-tariff barriers have been very strong and China uses non-tariff barriers unhesitatingly, whether it is in the name of phytosanitary measures or any other, for which due investigations can happen, for which due both sides sitting and talking can happen, but no progress is made," the Minister said.
Highlighting India's distinct approach to resolving trade frictions through dialogue rather than sudden retaliatory tariffs, she added that "it is not the way India believes in dealing with trade negotiations. We sit and talk. It is sometimes very tiresome. But we do go through that approach rather than put CVDs, countervailing duties or some non-tariff barriers to counter the non-tariff barriers on the other side. So these are ways in which we find it difficult to correct the imbalance which prevails between China and us."
Beyond bilateral relations with China, the Finance Minister also touched upon the much anticipated India-US trade agreement.
"I think recently, a day or two ago, the Indian Commerce Minister has also spoken that they expect and wish to have the [India-US] agreement signed soon. Negotiations have been going on, I hope, in the interest of global trade and in the interest of trade between the two partners, India and US, the trade agreement gets concluded at the earliest," she noted.
Sitharaman also reiterated India's commitment to multilateralism while actively pursuing direct trade agreements with key partners, including the United Arab Emirates, Australia, Canada, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) bloc, alongside ongoing efforts to finalize a pact with the United States. (ANI)

high_priority_articles.summary: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic opportunity, economic imperative or geopolitical gamble?  MyJoyOnline
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Audio By Carbonatix
Walk through Abossey Okai, Tema and other industrial enclaves in Ghana and you can already see BRICS in Ghana's economy: spare parts and machinery from Guangzhou, pharmaceuticals and vehicles from India, gold flowing out to Dubai.
Samuel Okudzeto Abalakwa, Ghana’s Foreign Affairs Minister, announced cabinet’s approval for Ghana’s application to join the BRICS, at a joint press briefing with India’s External Affairs Minister during his visit to Accra. The Honourable Minister linked the decision to the President’s “New Economy” agenda and the desire for Ghana to chart its own path without being constrained by the conditionalities of a few international institutions. This announcement formalises a relationship that trade data has been describing for years.
The open questions are what formal membership adds, what it might cost, and how businesses should position themselves while the process plays out. The conversation is more relevant now, as Ghana transitions from a period of macroeconomic stabilisation towards one focused on investment-led growth and structural transformation.
Understanding BRICS and Why It Matters
What began in the early 2000s as an economic acronym coined to describe the fast-growing emerging economies of Brazil, Russia, India and China has evolved into one of the most influential geopolitical and economic blocs in the world. South Africa joined the grouping in 2010, transforming BRIC into BRICS and providing Africa with representation within the bloc. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE later joined, followed by Indonesia in 2025, bringing membership to 11, with Nigeria and several other countries holding partner status.
The group’s main institution is the New Development Bank (NDB), headquartered in Shanghai. The bank has approved over 120 projects worth about US$40 billion and admits new members on the condition that the founding BRICS countries' capital share never falls below 55%. One stated ambition - reducing reliance on the US Dollar - remains a key aspiration yet to be realised.
BRICS today is no longer simply a forum for emerging economies. It represents a broader vision for increasing the influence of developing nations within global governance structures. For many countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America, the appeal of BRICS lies not in replacing existing global institutions, but in creating additional options. In an increasingly uncertain global environment characterised by economic fragmentation, geopolitical competition and shifting trade dynamics, diversification has become a strategic necessity.
Why Ghana Is Looking Towards BRICS
Ghana's interest in BRICS comes at a pivotal moment in its economic journey.
Following years of economic turbulence, debt restructuring and IMF-supported reforms, the Country has made notable progress in restoring macroeconomic stability. Economic discussions are increasingly shifting from stabilisation towards growth, productivity, investment and industrialisation. Internal economic briefings and policy discussions increasingly focus on how Ghana can move from recovery to sustainable private-sector-led growth.
At the same time, the global economic environment is changing. Emerging markets are playing a larger role in global trade and investment flows, while developing countries are seeking greater influence within international institutions.
Against this backdrop, BRICS presents Ghana with an opportunity to expand its economic options.
Government officials have publicly framed the proposed membership as part of a broader strategy to diversify international partnerships and create new avenues for cooperation. This rationale aligns closely with the Country's broader ambitions around industrialisation, infrastructure development, job creation and economic transformation.
The Economic Case for Membership
The strongest arguments in favour of Ghana joining BRICS are arguably economic rather than political. Four key areas of potential benefit to Ghana have been highlighted below:
- Alignment with where Ghana's trade already goes: This is the strongest economic argument. In 2025, the UAE took 25.9% of Ghana's exports, India 16.0%, South Africa 10.3% and China 4.9%. All four are BRICS members, which means roughly 57% of Ghana's export earnings already flow to the bloc. On the import side, China remained Ghana's largest supplier at about 23% of imports in the fourth quarter of 2025. Membership could institutionalise relationships that are already central to Ghana's balance of payments, while opening additional channels for exports and investment promotion.
- Development financing options: Ghana has completed a demanding IMF programme and now engages the Fund through a Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI), a non-financing arrangement that offers technical support and policy guidance. With no IMF money on the table, access to the NDB for infrastructure financing (energy, rail, water, digital) would widen the menu of long-tenor capital at a time when Ghana needs to finance growth. These investments will be essential if the Country is to realise its ambition of becoming a competitive industrial economy.
- Industrial and technology partnerships: The visit by India’s External Affairs Minister itself showed what is on offer, with plans announced to deepen cooperation in railways, pharmaceuticals, ICT, defence, agriculture and science and technology. If Ghana uses membership to negotiate local value addition, such as gold refining, cocoa processing and pharmaceutical manufacturing, rather than simply more raw commodity exports, the growth dividend could be real.
- Negotiating leverage: Being in more rooms strengthens Ghana's hand with every partner, including the Bretton Woods institutions, on debt treatment, climate finance and conditionality, amongst others.
Lessons from Africa's BRICS Experience
To understand what BRICS membership could mean for Ghana, it is important to examine the experiences of African countries already within the bloc.
South Africa's journey offers perhaps the most relevant case study. Since joining BRICS in 2010, South Africa has used the platform to deepen trade and investment relationships, expand diplomatic influence and access development financing through the New Development Bank. The NDB's first South African loan in 2016 supported renewable energy, and the bank has since backed 13 projects there worth around US$9 billion (in current terms), including a loan of up to US$1 billion for water and sanitation infrastructure under the Municipal Infrastructure Grant programme. The lesson is that the NDB can be a meaningful infrastructure financier for a member with a strong project pipeline and capable state entities. The Country continues to benefit from this association, while simultaneously maintaining strong economic relationships with Europe and the United States.
Ethiopia, which joined in 2024, presents a cautionary story. At admission, one Ethiopian economist judged that the direct economic benefit would be modest, but that membership would improve investor perception and widen options for development finance. Ethiopian analysts have observed that the country's trade and investment ties are stronger with individual BRICS countries such as China, Saudi Arabia and India than with the bloc as a whole, and that membership has not offset the AGOA benefits and Western privileges that were lost. The Ethiopian Economics Association also warned that trading in local currencies could worsen forex constraints and complicate Dollar-based trade with other partners, recommending that Ethiopia manages it relationship with both BRICS and the West in the short run to the benefit of the country.
Perhaps the most important lesson from these experiences is that BRICS membership itself does not create economic transformation. Membership rewards countries that come with bankable projects and strong institutions, and it does not by itself replace Western market access. South Africa's gains did not emerge simply because it joined BRICS; they emerged because the country actively leveraged membership to attract investment, strengthen trade relationships and promote national economic priorities.
The challenges and considerations
While the economic opportunities are compelling, it would be naïve to assume that BRICS membership comes without risks.
- Western Economic Relationships management is an immediate risk: The European Union, United States and United Kingdom remain among Ghana's most important development partners, export destinations and sources of foreign direct investment. President Trump has threatened additional tariffs on countries that align with what he describes as the bloc's anti-American policies. Even though Ghana’s bilateral goods trade with the US is not relatively huge, it matters disproportionately for specific sectors. With AGOA renewal and trade negotiations unsettled, the timing requires careful diplomacy. Ghana's engagement with BRICS should not be interpreted as a pivot away from the West. Such a framing creates a false choice. The world's most successful middle-income economies typically pursue diversified international relationships rather than exclusive alliances. The strategic objective should be to broaden Ghana's options, not narrow them.
- Trade imbalance and import competition: Concerns have been raised on whether Ghana, as a largely import-driven economy, risks becoming a dumping ground for larger BRICS producers such as China. Trade defence and local-content policies must be reviewed to ensure Ghanaian manufacturers are not squeezed in the pursuit of deeper integration.
- Choice of membership tier: The membership option being considered is of significant strategic importance. There have been questions around why Ghana is not following Nigeria's route as a BRICS partner country rather than seeking full membership. Legislators have also asked for scrutiny of the conditions attached to BRICS-linked financi

high_priority_articles.title: Europe’s debt map flips: Belgium borrows like Greece as France pays more than Italy - AOL.co.uk
high_priority_articles.summary: Europe’s debt map flips: Belgium borrows like Greece as France pays more than Italy  AOL.co.uk
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Imagine an investor who fell asleep in the summer of 2012, at the height of the euro crisis, and woke up this morning. He would remember a simple map. In the north, a core of countries that borrowed cheaply, with Germany at the centre. In the south, a periphery of debtors – Greece, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Ireland – that paid dearly for the privilege of staying in the single currency. Fourteen years later, that map no longer describes the eurozone.
Belgium, home to the European Union institutions, now borrows for ten years at 4.29%. Greece, bailed out three times, pays 4.35%, almost the same rate. Portugal, rescued in 2011, pays less than Spain. Ireland, rescued in 2010, pays almost the same as the Netherlands. And France, which he remembered as part of the core, pays more than Italy.
The old periphery has moved north. That is the backdrop against which eurozone governments are about to ask investors for more money than ever before.
What moved the border
Bond yields are the interest rates a government pays to borrow. They rise when investors think a country will need more money than it can comfortably repay, and they fall when it proves the opposite. Greece has spent a decade proving the opposite.
In 2025, Athens ran a budget surplus of 1.7% of gross domestic product (GDP), and its debt, though still the highest in Europe, fell by more than nine percentage points of GDP in a single year.
“For years, when markets talked about sovereign risk in Europe, the focus was usually on the periphery,” Ken Egan, head of European sovereign credit at the rating agency KBRA, told Euronews.
Over the past decade, he said, those countries have followed more prudent fiscal policy, improved their primary balances, extended debt maturities, collected taxes better through digitalisation and rebuilt their banks.
“That has helped smooth refinancing risks and put debt on a much firmer path than 10 or 15 years ago.”
Belgium went the other way. Its deficit widened to 5.2% of GDP last year, larger than France’s 5.1% in the same year, and its debt rose above 109% of GDP in the first quarter of 2026, and investors noticed.
“The traditional core has changed as well, but in a different direction,” Egan said.
“In some cases there is less clarity around the policy path, more political uncertainty, rising structural spending pressures and much higher refinancing costs than governments had become used to during the low-rate period.”
France’s position on the map is defined by one figure above all: the state spends 57.2% of everything the economy produces, the highest share in the G20. Debt has reached €3.6 trillion, or 119% of GDP, up from 98.2% before the pandemic.
The bill due in 2027
On 29 September, the French Treasury set out how much it will need to borrow next year: €340 billion in medium- and long-term bonds, a record, equal to about 11% of GDP and up from €310 billion this year.
Much of it is not new spending but old debt coming back for refinancing, as bonds issued during the pandemic and the energy crisis mature.
Every euro of that debt is being renewed at a higher price.
France has paid an average interest rate of 3.55% on medium- and long-term bonds issued so far this year, up from 3.14% last year. Its annual interest bill is forecast to rise from €62.6 billion in 2026 to €72.9 billion in 2027, roughly a fifth of what the state collected in revenue last year.
That last number is the one investors now read first.
“Markets are looking much more closely at the fiscal story, and not just at how much governments are borrowing, but what they are borrowing for,” Egan said.
“Borrowing that supports investment and future growth is one thing; borrowing mainly to cover a rising interest bill is viewed quite differently.”
Germany is issuing a record €512 billion of securities this year, but to pay for defence and infrastructure, which is the kind of borrowing markets forgive.
Italy and Spain will each refinance several hundred billion.
And the IMF, in its latest World Economic Outlook, pointed to a detail that makes every government more exposed: in the G7 and Spain, nearly 30% of public debt now matures within a year, so a change in interest rates reaches the budget within months rather than decades.
Why sovereign yields keep rising
Between February and September, the average 10-year yield across the G7 rose by more than a full percentage point to its highest level in nearly two decades, the IMF’s fiscal chief Rodrigo Valdés and his deputy Era Dabla-Norris wrote this week.
The oil shock, persistent inflation and the money pouring into artificial intelligence all played a part. But at the centre, they wrote, are fiscal fundamentals: investors demand more to lend for ten years to governments that keep spending more than they collect.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has added to the cost, raising its deposit rate twice this year to 2.50% to contain inflation.
The German 10-year yield, the floor for the whole eurozone, has climbed from 2.64% in February to 3.45%. France’s has risen twice as fast and briefly touched 5% in early October, the widest gap with Germany since 2012.
The danger, Egan said, is that the market itself becomes part of the problem.
“A political headline or weak budget can push the curve higher, refinancing becomes more expensive, fiscal space narrows, and the market then has another reason to demand a higher premium.”
That loop turns faster than it used to, because the buyers have changed.
For a decade the ECB bought government bonds with newly created money; now it lets them run off.
“There is less natural long-duration demand in the market, with central banks stepping back, pension demand changing and more of the marginal buying coming from price-sensitive investors,” Egan said. Higher energy prices, he added, make it worse by “weakening growth while keeping inflation and rates higher”.
The IMF describes the result in one sentence: in a growing number of countries, the interest rate on new debt is now higher than the growth rate of the economy.
When that happens, debt rises on its own unless the government runs a surplus before interest.
Most of Europe does not. “The more countries wait, the more painful the adjustment becomes,” the Fund wrote.
Is this 2012 again?
Not yet, says Lombard Odier. The Swiss bank’s investment office argues that markets are “pricing uncertainty rather than the conditions for a new sovereign debt crisis”. France’s interest payments remain affordable, at slightly above 2% of GDP, half Italy’s.
Its current account deficit is small, and it does not depend on foreign money the way Portugal, Spain and Greece did in 2012, when they imported capital worth 7% to 12% of their economies every year.
The bank’s forecast is dull rather than dramatic: French spreads stay wide until a credible budget passes parliament, probably not before the May 2027 presidential election, and the euro drifts lower, to $1.09.
Clara Raposo, vice-governor of the Banco de Portugal, offered a different warning this month.
Sovereign bond markets, she said, have become more sensitive to inflation, fiscal doubts and geopolitics, and shocks now spread faster from one country to another, amplified by funds that sell first and ask questions later.
“Trust may be intangible, but its economic consequences are real,” Raposo said.
Your debt, my inflation
The transmission is not only financial.
A randomised experiment with German firms in the Bundesbank’s panel, which surveys roughly 7,000 firms, published by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) earlier this year, found that half of them think the ECB will hold back on rate rises to protect weaker treasuries.
When researchers showed them a pessimistic forecast for the average debt-to-GDP ratio of France, Italy and Spain, the firms raised their expectations for German inflation three years ahead by 1.4 percentage points among those who distrust the ECB.
Fiscal stress in one member state, in other words, can raise inflation expectations in another, and the channel is trust.
In 2012, the question was whether the periphery could pay. In 2027, the question is who, exactly, the periphery is.

high_priority_articles.title: France and Germany strike deal to boost Europe's struggling car industry - Modern Ghana
high_priority_articles.summary: France and Germany strike deal to boost Europe's struggling car industry  Modern Ghana
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The deal between Europe's two economic powerhouses aims to cut carbon emissions and support the development and manufacture of electric cars in Europe, the two countries said in a joint statement published on Friday.
"Our shared amibition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe," it said.
The deal also provides "concrete incentives for investment, research and development, European production and resilient supply chains".
The agreement still needs the backing of other EU states and the European Parliament to become law, but is expected to shape the continent's future policy.
European car manufacturers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts, which have been increasingly targeting Europe as they face barriers to selling in the United States and weaker demand at home.
Chinese electric vehicles and hybrids accounted for 10.7 percent of the European market in the second quarter of 2026, up from 5.7 percent a year earlier, Schmidt Automotive Research said.
Franco-German dynamic
Paris and Berlin had long been at loggerheads on the course Europe should take as it seeks to revive its struggling auto industry.
Germany wanted less stringent carbon emission targets for carmakers and a broad interpretation of "made in Europe" to include key non-EU trade partners, such as Norway and the UK.
France, on the other hand, had pushed to preserve the bloc's climate ambitions and to keep the "made in Europe" public procurement scheme within the scope of EU member states.
Both countries' leaders welcomed the deal.
French President Emmanuel Macron said it showed a "clear ambition to successfully transform" the European automotive industry while upholding Europe's climate goals.
"We hope that this Franco-German dynamic will lead to a swift agreement with our partners, for the sake of our jobs and our industry," he wrote in a post on social media platform X.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz described the deal as a "good day for car drivers and for jobs in Germany, France and Europe".
"This sends a pro-investment signal to the industry," he wrote, also on X.
Softened emissions targets
The European Commission proposed last year that CO2 emissions from cars should drop by 90 percent from 2021 levels in 2035, and that carmakers would have to close the gap to 100 percent by using low-carbon steel and alternative fuels.
However, under the Franco-German deal, the target would be set at 90 percent without the need for any other compensatory measures.
The softened target is broadly in line with the wishes of German car manufacturers.
The deal also opens the door for cars running on renewable fuels to count as "zero-emission" and makes it much easier for automakers to reach CO2 targets.
'Good news' for the UK
The provisional Franco-German plan says that, for the automotive sector, the "Made in EU" label should cover the EU's 27 member states and other European partners that were part of the EU internal market on 1 January, 2020.
That would include the UK, which officially left the EU single market on 31 January, 2020.
An official at UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's office said it would be good news for the UK's automotive sector if it was included in the "Made in EU" scheme. He added, however, that the Franco-German proposal would need European consensus and that details were yet to be seen.
The Franco-German plan also says this inclusion should be subject to an agreement on full reciprocity, along with "dynamic alignment with EU conditions for investment from third countries and with EU trade protection measures".
That could mean the UK having to adopt the measures the EU has taken to limit imports of Chinese-built hybrid and battery electric vehicles.

high_priority_articles.title: Germany and France want own ‘Made in Europe’ rules for cars, outside EU industrial policy - EUobserver
high_priority_articles.summary: Germany and France want own ‘Made in Europe’ rules for cars, outside EU industrial policy  EUobserver
high_priority_articles.full_text:
France and Germany want more detailed “Made in Europe” rules for electric cars, and want them split off from the rest of the EU’s flagship industrial law.
The Franco-German deal, agreed after months of haggling on the margins of the EU summit in Brussels late on Thursday (15 October), says both files should then be adopted “as fast as possible and simultaneously”.
That would split the most fought-over part from the rest of the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), which also sets “Made in EU” and low-carbon requirements for steel, cement, aluminium and clean-tech products such as batteries and solar panels.
Paris hopes the new car definition will serve as a benchmark for the rest of the IAA, which sets “Made in Europe” rules for steel, cement, aluminium and clean energy technologies.
But this still has to be negotiated with other member states, people familiar with the talks said.

“We are driven by a clear ambition: to successfully transform our automotive industry while upholding our climate goals and our production in Europe,” said French president Emmanuel Macron on social media, announcing the deal.
“This is an investment signal to industry,” said German chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Made in Europe
The paper comes as Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating six-month presidency, is wrapping up a third compromise text on the industrial plan, which Irish officials hope will reach final agreement by mid November.
Publicly, Paris and Berlin said on Friday that their car deal will not affect climate targets and that their course “remains unchanged”.
But the paper behind the deal shows the trade-off that’s been made. Berlin accepted France’s demand for stricter “Made in Europe” rules that apply to fewer countries, while Paris agreed to looser emission rules for carmakers, as Germany had wanted.
To count as “Made in Europe”, a car would have to clear thresholds that tighten over time, and only cars meeting these rules could be bought, leased or rented with public subsidies, or bought by public authorities.
From 2028, the car must be assembled in Europe, with at least 70 percent of total value creation in components - excluding the battery.

high_priority_articles.title: South Korea's KOSPI Plunges 8% as Samsung and SK Hynix Lead a Chip Rout - Startup Fortune
high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea's KOSPI Plunges 8% as Samsung and SK Hynix Lead a Chip Rout  Startup Fortune
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Seoul's circuit breakers tripped for the tenth time this year on October 15. By the end of the session, the two companies making the memory chips behind the AI boom had each lost a tenth of their value.
The Kospi tumbled 8% to 5,528.05 on Thursday, triggering South Korea's tenth market-wide circuit breaker of the year, according to a report from The Korea Herald. SK Hynix sank 11.35%, and Samsung Electronics dropped 9.70%. Samsung Electro-Mechanics, which supplies components for the same AI server boom, fell sharply as well.
You don't halt an entire national stock exchange over nothing. The selloff opened rough, down 5.59% at the bell, and kept sliding all morning. A sell-sidecar hit at 9:07 a.m., suspending index futures-linked program trades. By 12:38 p.m., the main circuit breaker kicked in and froze trading across the board for 20 minutes. When it reopened, the bleeding continued.
Here's the part that should worry anyone holding AI-adjacent stocks: this wasn't really about chip demand collapsing. It was about the cost of money. A hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation reading on October 14 pushed back bets on near-term Federal Reserve rate cuts, and that hit hardest at exactly the companies that have been borrowing the most to build AI infrastructure. CoreWeave's bond yields had already jumped toward 15% earlier in the week on the same fear. When financing costs rise, the math behind every chip megafab and every AI data center gets shakier, and investors in Seoul decided to sell first and ask questions later.
Samsung and SK Hynix didn't need a rate scare to feel exposed. Two days earlier, on October 12, shares in both companies had already slid after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies unveiled a new 4F² DRAM cell architecture at a conference in Shanghai. CXMT is targeting a server DDR5 module built on that design by the end of 2026. Samsung's own roadmap doesn't get there until 2028, according to industry estimates reported at the time.
South Korea's KOSPI crashed nearly 10% on June 23 after Broadcom's Q3 AI chip guidance of $16 billion missed Wall Street's $17.2 billion estimate, triggering a circuit breaker as Samsung and SK Hynix each fell more than 12%. The selloff exposed the KOSPI's dangerous concentration in two memory chip stocks and the fragility of a market priced for... - Broadcom guidance miss triggers Korean market - AI chip demand uncertainty spooks semiconductor
CXMT still holds less than 10% of global DRAM share against Samsung's roughly 39% and SK Hynix's 25%, and it has published no performance data or qualification results to back up the claim. The architecture itself is unproven at scale under the export controls that limit CXMT's access to advanced manufacturing tools. But the memory market doesn't need a Chinese rival to actually catch up this year. It just needs traders to believe the moat is two years thinner than they thought it was last month, and Samsung's and SK Hynix's stocks already carried the valuation of companies with no rival in sight.
Japan felt the contagion too. Kioxia, the memory maker spun out of Toshiba, sold off sharply the same day, a sign the selloff wasn't a Korea-only story but a read-through across the entire Asian memory supply chain that feeds Nvidia, Microsoft, and every other buyer racing to stock AI servers.
The same day, Taiwan told a different story
Here's the twist. While Seoul was tripping circuit breakers, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. held its own third-quarter earnings call, on the same Thursday, and the numbers it reported were not a crisis. TSMC posted record quarterly revenue of NT$1.494 trillion, up 50.9% from a year earlier, beating the top end of its own forecast. Nine-month revenue for 2026 hit NT$3.899 trillion, up 41.1% year over year. Management's message, in short: the AI chip boom isn't slowing down on the manufacturing side at all.
So which is it? Frankly, both readings can be true at once, and that's the uncomfortable part. TSMC makes the logic chips and sells to a broad base of customers who are still paying up for capacity. Samsung and SK Hynix sell memory, a market where a credible new entrant and a sudden spike in the cost of capital can both bite at the same time, even while the underlying demand for AI computing keeps climbing. The Kospi crash isn't proof that AI spending is cracking. It's proof that the stocks built on the assumption nothing could touch Korean memory dominance had very little room for bad news, and got two pieces of it in the same week.
Foreign investors had already been pulling back hard going into the crash, posting heavy net selling in South Korean equities in the prior session alone, alongside a jump in short-selling activity. That's capital voting with its feet before the circuit breaker ever tripped, and it's the clearest sign yet that the easy money in Korean chip stocks has started asking harder questions than it did a month ago.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
South Korea's third-quarter earnings season officially kicks off the week of October 19, and the recent deep correction in memory chip stocks is being viewed by Wall Street as a window for medium-term positioning. JPMorgan's Asia-Pacific equity research team concluded in its latest note that the memory sector has entered an "expectations reset quarter," and the current divergence between price and fundamentals offers investors an entry point to bet on an upcycle that is "longer and higher."
According to a research note published October 15 by JPMorgan analyst Jay Kwon and colleagues, last week's preliminary results from Samsung Electronics (in line), LG Electronics (below expectations), and LG Energy Solution (above expectations) set the tone for this earnings season. The report noted that after meeting with more than 100 investors across Asia, Kwon pointed out that memory stocks have fallen approximately 6% over the past month and 15% over the past three months, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) rose about 10% and fell about 4% over the same respective periods—a divergence that is creating a favorable risk-reward entry point for duration trades.
Hit by hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data overnight and mounting concerns over an AI valuation bubble, South Korean equities suffered a historic sell-off on October 15. Data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on October 14 showed September CPI rose 3.7% year-over-year, up from 3.4% previously, reigniting rate-hike fears; rising credit risk in AI infrastructure financing further amplified valuation concerns. South Korea's KOSPI closed at 5,554.22, down 7.57%, breaching the 5,600 level. Chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix led the decline, closing down more than 9% and 10%, respectively. The Korea Exchange activated a "sell-side sidecar" mechanism to halt programmatic sell orders and ease selling pressure.
The sell-off swept across major Asia-Pacific markets:
| Market | Close | Daily Change | 
|---|---|---|
| South Korea KOSPI | 5,554.22 | -7.57% | 
| South Korea KOSDAQ | 760.82 | -7.65% |

| Taiwan Weighted Index | 46,969.87 | -3.41% | 
Note: Closing data as of October 15, 2026. The Taiwan Weighted Index fell 1,655.96 points, the sixth-largest single-day point decline in Taiwan market history.
Taiwan's market was not spared either: the weighted index lost the 47,000 level and its monthly moving average, with foreign investors selling a record NT$302.555 billion (approximately $9.3 billion) in a single day. TSMC fell NT$50 to close at NT$2,440, while ASE Technology and other packaging and testing interface names closed limit-down.
Expectations reset quarter: duration trade logic amid sentiment divergence
Jay Kwon met with more than 100 Asian investors in Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, and Hong Kong over the past two weeks. The findings reveal a key divergence: top-down conclusions about AI spending sustainability are clearly disconnected from bottom-up readings of memory supply-demand fundamentals, with investor sentiment sharply split.
JPMorgan had previously characterized Q3 as an "expectations reset quarter," noting that memory stocks could remain volatile in the near term due to a lack of immediate catalysts. On the data front, memory stocks are down roughly 6% over the past month and 15% over three months, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose about 10% and fell about 4% over the same periods—a stark contrast in trajectories.
However, the bank believes this very sentiment divergence and price dislocation provides a good entry point for "duration trades"—bets on a memory upcycle that is "longer and higher" from a medium-term perspective. Kwon added that from a medium-term view, the risk-reward has turned favorable, and he recommends investors accumulate on dips during the recent pullback.
Six overweight picks spanning the memory supply chain
Based on this assessment, JPMorgan identified its core overweight picks for the next six months, covering memory chips themselves as well as upstream and downstream ecosystem plays:
| Name | Segment | Ticker | 
|---|---|---|
| Samsung Electronics | Memory core | 005930.KS | 
| SK Hynix | Memory core | 000660.KS | 
| Kioxia | Memory | 285A.T | 
| Samsung Electro-Mechanics | MLCC & substrates | 009150.KS | 
| ISU | AI PCB | 007660.KS | 
| ISC | Test sockets | 095340.KQ | 
Note: List sourced from JPMorgan's October 15 research note; overweight horizon is six months.
This portfolio reflects a systematic approach to positioning across the entire memory supply chain's medium-term recovery, rather than a single-segment bet. From memory manufacturers to passive components, PCBs, and test-related equipment, it covers the full hardware chain driven by AI compute expansion.
Kioxia, the only Japanese company on the list, also plunged in Tokyo trading that day: it closed at ¥12,880 (approximately $82), down 12.32% on the day, and has fallen more than 30% from its post-split high of ¥19,750 (approximately $130) set on October 5. The Nikkei 225 fell 3,318 points that day, its third-largest single-day point decline in history. Kioxia is scheduled to report earnings on October 30, shortly after South Korea's earnings season begins, providing another checkpoint for the memory cycle thesis.
Validation framework and falsification conditions
JPMorgan also laid out a validation framework for its thesis. On the results front, the key question is whether earnings delivery from technology and life insurance sectors—slated as outperformers—beats sectors the bank has flagged as negative, as results roll in starting the week of October 19. On the mechanism front, marginal changes in memory spot prices, AI-related orders, and capital expenditure will be critical indicators of whether the "longer upcycle" duration thesis holds.
The bank also spelled out clear falsification conditions: if memory supply-demand continues to weaken, catalysts remain absent, or the earnings season brings widespread downward revisions, JPMorgan said it would withdraw the thesis. The validation window runs from October 19, 2026 through early November.
The logic can be summarized as follows:
For the South Korean market overall, this quarter's earnings season will not only determine near-term pricing in the memory sector but also serve as a key reference point for the health of the global semiconductor supply chain. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, as the two memory giants, will see their earnings performance and capex guidance directly test whether the AI-driven memory upcycle remains on track.

high_priority_articles.summary: Budget, Ukraine, migration: Five takeaways from the EU leaders’ summit  EuronewsEU resists bid to weaken emissions rules as leaders spar over energy costs  Financial TimesCosta angers EU leaders as splits mar summit  POLITICO.euStatement by the President: EUCO of 16 October 2026  European CommissionEU member states struggle to reach an agreement to lower energy prices  Le Monde.fr
high_priority_articles.full_text:
EU leaders ended their Brussels summit with no deal on the budget, a new €70bn Ukraine funding gap, open clashes over energy and migration, but fresh resolve to create new trade defence tools to battle China.
EU leaders gathered in Brussels on Thursday and Friday with a packed agenda, from the long-term budget and financial support for Ukraine to migration, energy and China.
The summit alternated between entrenched positions on the bloc’s budget, a warm welcome for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and clashes over energy and migration policies.
Here are the five highlights.
Rallying behind Ukraine
The bitter row between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump dominated the second day of the summit.
Leaders closed ranks behind Zelenskyy and promised to keep sanctions in place for as long as Russia pursues its full-scale invasion. They also condemned the diesel deal struck by Trump with Russian President Vladimir Putin, although the Bulgarian prime minister broke ranks to support it.
The reception gave Zelenskyy a moment of diplomatic relief as Trump doubled down, claiming Zelenskyy was “more difficult” to deal with than Putin and demanding new elections in Ukraine. Trump also called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, its main leverage, a “disgrace”.
“I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively,” Zelenskyy said in a defiant tone. “We were attacked, occupied, and our people were killed. It is only logical that we have the right to defend ourselves.”
“We will keep living, fighting, and most importantly, living with dignity,” he added.
In his address, Zelenskyy asked leaders for an additional €70bn in financial and military support next year to counter Russia’s escalation.
The request upends the bloc’s plans, which assumed last year's €90bn loan would cover both 2026 and 2027. EU leaders tasked the Commission to come up with a proposal on how to address Kyiv's financial needs.
Filling the gap will be anything but easy. Soaring borrowing costs make joint debt unpalatable. The immobilised Russian assets, which Zelenskyy raised again, remain politically divisive. And bilateral contributions risk leaving the burden on a handful of wealthy countries.
EU budget
On Thursday, leaders debated the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) at length but, as expected, made little headway, as the “frugal” net contributors and the southern and eastern “Friends of Cohesion” dug in.
One thing is clear: the negotiating box tabled by the Irish presidency just days ago, which proposed slashing €141bn from the overall budget to appease the frugal, is now officially dead.
European Council President António Costa will take over the talks. He is due to present a new compromise in the coming weeks, which many expect to come before the special summit he has called for 26 November, just days before the Spanish elections.
Costa is expected to pursue three main lines: keep national contributions as low as possible, rework the package of EU-wide taxes, including by drawing on European Parliament proposals, and restore the flexibility instruments the Irish presidency ruthlessly cut.
That Costa would sooner or later step in was always on the cards. More worrying is that leaders on both sides now openly say they feel no pressure to close the deal by the end of the year.
Seasoned negotiators know that deadlines force concessions. Member states may be playing with fire: a no-deal in December would raise the prospect of talks slipping until after an electoral season that could reshape Europe’s political landscape.
Migration
Migration proved once again among the most contentious issues, after the last discussion, in June, descended into a shouting match between Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on one side and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen on the other.
This time, Rome unexpectedly extended a hand to Madrid just before the dossier reached the table on Friday. Italy and Spain reached what appears to be a first step towards ending their border dispute, after a string of tit-for-tat checks introduced in the wake of the Ceuta crisis.
Italy’s temporary border controls were due to expire on Thursday evening. They were extended by a week to align with Spain’s, which expire on 22 October. The two interior ministers are due to agree on replacement measures by then.
But while Meloni opened the summit in a conciliatory tone, Sánchez’s other main European nemesis, Frederiksen, did not spare her fellow social democrat over his plan to regularise the status of 600,000 migrants.
“I have asked the European Commission to examine what happens when a country does almost the exact opposite of what the rest of us are doing,” Frederiksen said, referring to Spain in all but name.
Meloni, Frederiksen and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten hosted an informal breakfast before the discussion with 17 other EU leaders to explore “innovative solutions” on migration. Support is growing for emergency measures allowing asylum applications to be suspended during crises.
Tensions between the migration hard-liners and Spain and France came to the fore as the Italian, Danish and Polish governments pushed to rewrite the conclusions to call for avoiding “measures that could create incentives for illegal migration.”
By contrast, the final text merely urges the Commission to coordinate with the member states "on all types of instrumentalisation."
China
On “macroeconomic imbalances”, EU jargon for avoiding naming China, leaders held their course despite the deal between the European Commission and Beijing to curb hybrid car imports.
Over lunch on Thursday, they pressed the Commission to prepare a toolbox of new trade defence instruments, including safeguards with quotas and tariffs, to shield the chemicals and machinery industries from Chinese competition.
China loomed large as the bloc faces a trade deficit of about €360bn with Beijing. Chemicals and machinery, among the sectors hardest hit by cheap Chinese imports, were singled out as the next industries needing urgent protection after the hybrid car quotas.
While the car quotas were negotiated with Beijing, leaders called on Thursday for unilateral safeguards to be introduced “without delay”, according to officials.
The Commission presented last week’s deal as the first phase of negotiations launched in June. But time is running out: the EU’s trade deficit with China keeps widening month after month, and Chinese customs data show Chinese exports to the EU up 25% over the past year.
The EU’s strategy is to keep talking as long as dialogue delivers concrete results, while strengthening its trade defences. France and Germany last week urged the Commission to develop a new instrument to respond swiftly to market disruptions caused by China, which has been accused of unfair trade practices.
“The competition must be fair. We will create instruments against leveraging capacities, against high subsidies, against undervalued currencies. And there will be a toolbox for that. The toolbox will be bigger. It will also be applied as necessary,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.
Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told leaders her institution would begin work on such a tool, though it remains unclear whether it will be ready before the end of the year.
Other instruments are in the pipeline, including a diversification tool to encourage EU companies to diversify their suppliers of strategic products such as critical raw materials, and a solidarity mechanism to help member states hit by possible Chinese countermeasures.
Energy
On Thursday, leaders were dragged into an interminable discussion on energy. The Visegrád Group (V4) and Italy asked to amend the summit conclusions to call on the Commission to propose new measures to curb short-term swings in electricity prices and to reassess the proposed Emissions Trading System (ETS).
The V4, Italy and, to a lesser extent, Greece led the push because they face some of Europe’s highest energy costs, a concern largely shared by other member states, which ultimately called for a coordinated European response to the ongoing energy crisis.
The attempt to reopen the ETS, however, triggered an ideological backlash from Finland, Denmark and Sweden. The system makes companies pay for their emissions and encourages investment in sustainability.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, by contrast, lashed out at the carbon tax, accusing it of wrecking Europe’s competitiveness by fuelling soaring energy costs for the benefit of market speculators.
“We’ve been engaged in a drafting exercise all day at the leaders’ level about something technical,” an EU official vented at the margins of the summit. “It’s not resulting in any new measures or new policies that actually help EU member states in their problems.”
Rome and the V4 know they lack the qualified majority to reopen the EU’s carbon market rules. The aim was rather to signal to domestic audiences that they are doing what they can to contain the surge in energy prices.

EU Greenwashing Rules Take Effect With Fines Exceeding 4% of Turnover
- Financial exposure: EU Member States can impose greenwashing penalties exceeding 4% of annual turnover for serious breaches, depending on national enforcement rules.
- Stricter environmental claims: New restrictions prohibit unsubstantiated claims such as “eco” and “sustainable”, alongside carbon neutrality claims based on offsetting.
- Existing inventory: EU regulators have proposed a proportionate enforcement approach for products manufactured, ordered or distributed before the 27 September deadline.
EU Tightens Enforcement of Environmental Marketing Claims
Brussels has introduced stricter consumer protection rules targeting corporate greenwashing, exposing businesses to substantial financial penalties for misleading environmental claims.
The EU’s Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive (ECGT) became applicable on 27 September 2026. It prohibits several common environmental marketing practices, including unsupported sustainability labels and misleading carbon neutrality claims.
National authorities will oversee enforcement, with the most serious violations potentially attracting fines exceeding 4% of annual turnover.
EU regulators have also published a “common understanding” outlining a proportionate approach to existing inventory. The guidance addresses products manufactured, ordered, distributed or placed on retail shelves before the September deadline.
For multinational businesses, the changes create immediate compliance challenges across product packaging, advertising, sustainability communications and supply chains.
Generic Green Claims Face New Restrictions
The directive targets environmental claims that cannot be supported by recognised evidence.
Terms such as “eco” and “sustainable” face restrictions when companies cannot demonstrate the environmental performance implied by their marketing.
The legislation also prohibits claims suggesting products have neutral, reduced or positive greenhouse gas impacts based on carbon offsetting.
Corporate commitments concerning future environmental performance face additional scrutiny.
Companies advertising future “net zero” performance must support those claims with publicly available implementation plans. Independent experts must verify the commitments, with their findings made publicly accessible.
Businesses also cannot present compliance with minimum legal environmental requirements as a distinctive sustainability advantage.
These provisions increase pressure on marketing, legal and sustainability departments to align consumer-facing communications with verifiable environmental performance.
Existing Stock Receives Proportionate Regulatory Treatment
One of the most commercially significant developments concerns products already circulating through European supply chains.
EU regulators have proposed a proportionate approach to goods manufactured, ordered, distributed or stocked before 27 September.
The guidance recognises the practical difficulties of immediately replacing packaging and labels across extensive retail inventories.
However, this approach should not be interpreted as a blanket exemption from the new requirements.
Companies must distinguish between existing inventory and newly produced materials while monitoring how individual Member States apply enforcement measures.
For manufacturers and retailers, the distinction could influence inventory management, packaging expenditure and contractual arrangements with suppliers.
Packaging Rules Add Another Compliance Layer
The EU’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) introduced further restrictions from 12 August 2026.
Environmental claims concerning recyclability and recycled content must exceed minimum regulatory requirements.
Businesses must also clarify whether claims apply to individual packaging units or their broader packaging portfolios.

These obligations will evolve as additional PPWR provisions become applicable.
Companies operating across multiple European markets face increasing pressure to standardise environmental claims while accommodating national enforcement practices.
UK Advertising Rulings Reinforce Scrutiny
Regulatory action is also intensifying outside the EU.
The UK’s Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) recently ruled against travel agencies Thomas Cook, loveholidays and DialAFlight over inadequately explained environmental advertising claims.
Advertisements describing hotels as “eco” or “eco-conscious” failed to provide sufficient information about the environmental characteristics supporting those descriptions.
The ASA also upheld complaints against Eurowings and Qatar Airways concerning speculative carbon offsetting claims.
Regulators found that the advertisements could mislead consumers about the environmental impact of individual flights.
Meanwhile, the UK Law Commission is examining a potential consumer class actions regime. Its consultation closes on 30 October.
Such a framework could increase corporate litigation exposure for misleading sustainability claims.
Financial and Governance Implications for Global Businesses
The EU’s enforcement framework raises the financial consequences of unsupported environmental marketing.
For executives, compliance now extends beyond sustainability reporting into product development, procurement, advertising approvals and corporate governance.
Investors must also consider whether companies maintain adequate controls over environmental claims across international markets.
The combination of turnover-based penalties, stricter substantiation requirements and potential litigation creates material legal and reputational exposure.
For businesses selling into Europe, credible sustainability communication increasingly depends on documented performance rather than broad environmental positioning.
The EU’s approach could also influence regulatory expectations internationally, particularly as authorities examine the credibility of corporate climate commitments and consumer-facing environmental claims.
